courseDescription: An introductory college-level computing course that introduces students to the breadth of the field of computer science. Students learn to design and evaluate solutions and to apply computer science to solve problems through the development of algorithms and programs. They incorporate abstraction into programs and use data to find new knowledge. Students also explore how computing innovations and computing systems work, explore their potential impacts, and contribute to a vibrant, ethical, and collaborative computing culture.
targetLearner: High school students preparing for the AP Computer Science Principles Exam, as well as anyone seeking an intuitive, concept-first introduction to programming, digital data, algorithms, systems, networking, and the societal impacts of technology.

projects.project_name: AP CSP Prep Portfolio: Eco-Tracker Program and Digital Artifacts
projects.project_description: Throughout this course, you will build a complete AP Computer Science Principles portfolio. You will design, develop, and document a complete, interactive Python/Pseudocode simulation tool ('Eco-Tracker') that tracks individual carbon footprint metrics and tests environmental scenarios. Alongside this program, you will construct physical and logical network diagrams, design visual data representations, and draft a complete set of written responses matching the College Board AP CSP Create Performance Task requirements.
projects.final_deliverable: A comprehensive ZIP archive containing: (1) 'eco_tracker.py' program code with comments showing modular functions, algorithms, and data structures; (2) A 1-minute narrated video demonstrating program execution; (3) A written AP CSP Create Task preparation document outlining procedural and data abstraction; (4) A digital data analysis report with custom infographics; and (5) A network protocol mapping diagram.

units.title: Creative Development
units.description: This unit focuses on the iterative, creative processes of program development and collaboration. Students will understand how computing innovations solve real-world problems, how programmers design and refine software, and how to successfully plan and construct the official AP Create Performance Task.

lectures.title: Computing and Creative Problem-Solving
lectures.description: Explore the fundamental nature of computing innovations, understand program purposes, and learn how to collaborate effectively to design solutions for diverse users.

sessions.title: Computing Innovations
sessions.description: Define what constitutes a computing innovation, distinguishing between its physical, non-physical, and conceptual components.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Start the lecture on a clear, clean whiteboard by posing a deceptively simple question: What makes a device or tool a 'computing innovation'? Draw two columns on the board. On the left side, sketch a traditional mechanical analog wristwatch. On the right, sketch a modern smartwatch. Explain to the students that while both keep time, only the smartwatch is a computing innovation because it relies on computer code, data representation, and program logic to function. Instruct teachers to write down the formal definition: a computing innovation is any innovation that includes a computer or program code as an integral part of its functionality. Highlight that this definition is crucial for the AP CSP framework, as students often mistake purely mechanical or electronic inventions (like a basic flashlight) for computing innovations.

Now, divide the whiteboard into three distinct horizontal lanes labeled Physical, Non-Physical, and Conceptual. Use the smartwatch example to populate these lanes, showing how they form a complete system. In the Physical lane, write down sensors, processors, and touchscreens. In the Non-Physical lane, list the operating system, the mobile app code, and wireless transmission protocols. In the Conceptual lane, write down the health-tracking service and data analytics. This visual breakdown directly addresses a common student misconception: that computing innovations are strictly physical gadgets. By visualizing these layers, students will understand that pure software—such as a ride-sharing algorithm or a social media feed system—is just as much a computing innovation as a physical robot.

Transition to the logical engine that powers every single computing innovation: the Input-Process-Output (IPO) model. On the center of the whiteboard, draw a large, directional flow diagram with three boxes: Input, Process, and Output. Explain that data must enter the system (Input), undergo some transformation or calculation (Process), and then produce a result or action (Output). Walk through a smart thermostat innovation to demonstrate this: the input is the ambient temperature sensor reading or a user setting a target temperature via an app; the process is the internal computer checking if the current temperature is lower than the target; the output is the signal sent to turn on the heating system. This systematic tracing establishes a foundational mental model that prepares students for programming logic in Unit 3.

Conclude the session with an interactive whiteboard challenge to check for understanding. Write down two scenarios on the board: a mechanical combination padlock and a smart biometric door lock. Ask the class to first identify which of the two is the computing innovation and justify why. Once they correctly isolate the smart biometric lock, have them come up to the board or sketch on their own notebooks the IPO model for this lock. Guide them to list inputs like fingerprint scans or keypad presses, the matching algorithm as the process, and the physical unlocking mechanism or a push notification sent to a phone as the output. Use this moment to clarify that physical parts, like the steel bolt of the lock, are not the innovation itself, but are controlled by the computing elements.

tasks: Identify whether a given technology meets the criteria of a computing innovation.
Analyze an innovation to identify its inputs, processes, and outputs.

sessions.title: Program Purpose and Function
sessions.description: Differentiate between a program's overall purpose (the problem it solves) and its specific function (how it behaves).
sessions.sessionOutline:
Begin the session by drawing a thick, vertical dividing line down the center of the physical or virtual whiteboard. On the left side, write the word 'Purpose' in large letters, and on the right side, write 'Function.' To establish an immediate, intuitive grasp of this core AP CSP distinction, explain that every piece of software is created with a human-centric 'Why' (the purpose) and a technical 'What' or 'How' (the function). Use a non-software physical analogy first, such as a simple mechanical alarm clock. The purpose of the alarm clock is to help people wake up on time so they are not late for school or work. The function of the clock is to keep track of time incrementally and emit a loud, vibrating buzz when the internal gears align with the set alarm hand. This mechanical distinction primes students to look past raw code mechanics to see the human motivation behind development.

Transition the whiteboard visualization from the mechanical clock to a modern software example, such as a ride-sharing app. On the left under 'Purpose,' write: 'To provide convenient, reliable, and safe transportation options for urban commuters who do not own cars.' Explain that this addresses a human pain point and represents the overarching goal of the system. On the right side under 'Function,' write: 'Calculates the shortest route between two GPS coordinates, processes credit card payments, and sends push notifications to drivers.' Guide students to see that the code doesn't directly 'solve' the transportation problem on its own; rather, its specific technical actions and calculations collectively work together to fulfill that broader purpose. Emphasize that on the AP Exam, questions will test this boundary by asking students to classify program descriptions.

A major student misconception to address here is the tendency to mistake a program's output for its purpose. Students often think that if a program outputs a calculated number, that calculation is the purpose. To preemptively correct this, write a scenario on the board: 'An application that allows users to input their daily water intake and displays a progress bar towards their target.' Point out that 'displaying the progress bar' is a function, while 'encouraging users to stay healthy and hydrated' is the true purpose. Show how the function is the computational vehicle that carries us toward the destination, which is the purpose.

Conclude the session with a collaborative whiteboarding practice. Present a descriptive paragraph of a hypothetical mobile application designed for local community gardens to coordinate tool sharing. Write several disconnected statements on the board, such as 'Allows users to search for available lawnmowers,' 'Fosters community collaboration and reduces individual purchasing costs,' and 'Sends an email alert when a borrowed tool is overdue.' Have students analyze these statements. Guide them to categorize the search and email alerts as specific functions (the actions the software executes) and the community building/cost reduction as the purpose (the human benefit). This active categorization equips students to approach similar AP stimulus questions with a critical, analytical lens.

tasks: Examine a program's description and categorize statements as describing its function versus its purpose.

sessions.title: Identifying User Needs
sessions.description: Learn how user requirements and accessibility standards shape software design and drive development priorities.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Begin the session by writing a bold statement on the board: "We do not build software for ourselves; we build it for the world." This session pivots from the abstract concepts of computing innovations to the deeply human discipline of user-centric design. Introduce the concept-first model of software development by drawing a simple timeline showing how user needs must precede code. Explain that when developers skip this discovery phase, they fall victim to the "I am the user" fallacy—assuming that because they find an interface intuitive, everyone else will. This bias is a major pitfall in AP CSP, and highlighting it early sets up the logical chain of user-driven design.

Next, split the whiteboard into two columns: "User Pain Points" and "Program Requirements." On the left side, write down a raw, unstructured piece of user feedback from an imaginary ride-sharing app, such as: "I can't use this app when it's sunny outside, and the buttons are too small for my fingers when I'm in a hurry." Use this real-world scenario to explain how vague human frustrations are translated into clear, actionable, and testable developer instructions. On the right column, systematically map these pain points to three formal program requirements: high-contrast visual modes, dynamic text-scaling options, and a minimum clickable button size of 48x48 pixels. This visual mapping teaches students that requirements must be specific and verifiable.

Now, introduce the concept of Accessibility (often abbreviated as A11y) as a non-negotiable standard rather than an afterthought. Draw a conceptual spectrum on the board showing how accessibility features designed for permanent disabilities (like visual impairment) also benefit users with temporary limitations (like glare from the sun) or situational constraints (like holding a baby while using an app). Detail key accessibility benchmarks such as screen-reader compatibility, alt-text for images, and color-blind-friendly palettes. Emphasize that inclusive software design is not just an ethical duty but a technical requirement that expands a product's market reach and usability.

Conclude with an interactive design simulation on the whiteboard. Present a scenario where a local library needs a book-reservation portal used heavily by both young children and senior citizens. Guide the class to identify potential barriers for these two demographics. Have the teacher lead students in drafting three distinct, concrete program requirements addressing color contrast, cognitive simplicity, and touch-target sizes based on this scenario. This practice moment ensures students can confidently translate qualitative user stories into quantitative software specifications, bridging the gap between empathy and engineering.

tasks: Analyze a scenario of user feedback and draft three program requirements to address their pain points.

sessions.title: Collaboration in Computing
sessions.description: Examine the benefits of diverse teams, peer programming, and feedback cycles in creating robust, unbiased computing innovations.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this session by dismantling the pervasive myth of the 'lone programmer' working in a dark basement. On the whiteboard, draw a single isolated figure versus a dynamic, connected web of diverse individuals. Explain that modern computing innovations are far too complex for any single mind to construct without introducing blind spots. A diverse development team brings varied life experiences, cultural perspectives, and technical insights. This diversity is not just a social benefit; it is a technical safeguard. Diverse teams actively prevent algorithmic bias—such as facial recognition systems failing on certain skin tones or voice assistants ignoring regional accents—by questioning assumptions during the design phase before a single line of code is written.

Next, introduce the formalized concept of pair programming, visualizing it on the board as a two-person vehicle. Define the two distinct roles: the 'Driver' and the 'Navigator.' The Driver is at the keyboard, focusing on the immediate, low-level mechanics of writing syntactically correct code. The Navigator sits beside them, looking at the bigger picture, anticipating logical errors, checking the code against requirements, and planning the next steps. Address the common student misconception that pair programming is inefficient or 'halves productivity' because two people are working on one computer. Explain how, in reality, pair programming significantly reduces debugging time and produces cleaner, more robust code because continuous peer review occurs in real-time, catching bugs before they are compiled.

Transition to the core cognitive benefit of this collaborative dynamic: how it fosters creative problem-solving and reduces bugs. Use the whiteboard to trace a simple debugging scenario. Show how a solitary programmer might get stuck in a cognitive loop, staring at their own logic error (such as an off-by-one error in a loop) because our brains tend to see what we *intended* to write rather than what we *actually* wrote. With a partner, the Navigator's fresh eyes immediately break this loop. Furthermore, dialogue between the Driver and Navigator forces them to articulate their thoughts out loud, a process that often leads to spontaneous breakthroughs and creative, out-of-the-box programming solutions.

To consolidate these ideas, prompt the class with an active reflection scenario: Ask students to analyze a situation where a software team is tasked with building an app to help elderly users track health metrics. Have them explain how implementing pair programming and structured feedback cycles during development would prevent usability issues. Guide them to articulate that the immediate feedback of a partner ensures accessibility standards are upheld, while the collaborative design prevents developer-centric assumptions, ultimately producing a far more resilient and user-friendly product.

tasks: Explain how pair programming reduces errors and produces more creative code.

lectures.title: Program Design and Development
lectures.description: Dive into software engineering practices. Learn to set requirements, design specifications, code iteratively, and systematically test and debug your projects.

sessions.title: Defining Program Requirements
sessions.description: Understand how to formulate clear, measurable program specifications before writing any code.
sessions.sessionOutline:
To begin this lecture on Program Design and Development, the teacher will write a simple, provocative question on the physical or virtual whiteboard: 'How do we know we've built the right thing?' This session grounds students in the absolute starting point of any computer science project—defining program requirements before touching a single line of code. The teacher will outline why jump-starting directly into programming leads to catastrophic design failures, introducing the concept of a program specification as a contract between the developer, the user, and the problem itself. By framing this visually, students understand that a requirement is not just a feature list, but a precise, measurable benchmark of success.

Next, the teacher will bifurcate the whiteboard into two columns to introduce the foundational distinction between Functional Requirements and Non-Functional Requirements. The teacher will explain that functional requirements define *what* the system must do (e.g., inputs, operations, outputs, and data transformations), while non-functional requirements define *how* the system behaves under constraints (e.g., performance, usability, security, and accessibility). Using an intuitive analogy like building a car, the teacher can explain that 'the car must have four wheels and steer left or right' is functional, whereas 'the car must accelerate to 60 mph in under 5 seconds' is non-functional. A major misconception here is that students often write vague goals like 'the program should be easy to use' or 'the software must run fast.' The teacher must actively combat this by showing how to translate subjective desires into testable, objective statements, such as specifying actual numeric constraints and explicit user interactions.

To apply this logic immediately, the teacher will transition to a live-drafting whiteboard exercise focused on a simple calculation tool, such as a split-the-bill or tip calculator. The teacher will lead the class through a step-by-step breakdown: defining what specific inputs the user must provide (e.g., total bill amount, tip percentage, number of people), what validations are necessary (e.g., rejecting negative numbers or division-by-zero errors), and what the exact calculated outputs must be. The teacher will sketch a flow diagram on the board mapping inputs to operations to outputs, visually isolating potential edge cases. This hands-on drafting highlights why rigorous requirements act as a preventive debugging tool—by resolving logical ambiguities on the whiteboard first, students avoid writing buggy code that they would otherwise have to refactor later. The session concludes by connecting these drafted requirements to the upcoming design phase, preparing students to convert these static specifications into active program logic.

tasks: Draft functional requirements for a simple calculation tool.

sessions.title: Designing a Program
sessions.description: Study software design strategies, including flowcharts, user stories, and modular planning techniques.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this session by addressing a major misconception among beginner developers: that programming is purely an exercise in writing code. To correct this, we introduce 'Designing a Program' as the vital blueprint phase that bridges the gap between raw requirements and active development. The teacher should sketch a comparison on the whiteboard showing a house built without blueprints versus one built with a detailed structural layout. This establishes the logical chain that thinking before coding prevents messy, unmanageable logic loops later. We introduce the core tools of program design: flowcharts for logical branching, user stories for capturing functional requirements from an end-user's perspective, and modular planning to break a complex problem into smaller, isolated components. Special emphasis is placed on user stories as a technique for clarifying exactly what needs to be programmed, ensuring that students never lose sight of user intent during implementation.

Moving deeper into technical visualization, the teacher will introduce a standardized whiteboard diagramming notation. We establish three fundamental flowchart symbols: rectangles for process steps or assignments, diamonds for decision-making logic (conditionals), and ovals for start and end terminals. The teacher will demonstrate how these shapes map directly to subsequent programming structures. For instance, a diamond element directly maps to an 'if/else' block in pseudocode. The critical logic path to explain here is flow control—how a program moves step-by-step and branches based on inputs. To prevent the common student trap of creating endless or disconnected flowchart loops, the teacher must explicitly model how to design a complete path with a guaranteed termination point.

Next, we introduce a classroom practice scenario: mapping out the logical flow for a simple mobile alarm application that snooze-controls based on user inputs. The teacher will guide students to write down user stories for this app first, then translate those goals into a clear flowchart diagram. During this process, the teacher should actively point out how a loop is formed when the user hits 'snooze' and how the program breaks that loop once a timer expires or the 'dismiss' action is triggered. This highlights the value of modular design, showing how a sub-routine like 'play alarm tone' can be kept as a separate reusable block rather than being re-created multiple times within the flowchart.

To wrap up the session, the teacher leads a reflection on how these visual representations protect developers from logic errors. We analyze a diagnostic scenario where an unmapped loop runs infinitely, contrast it with our cleanly designed flowchart, and show how the diagram acts as a debugging map before code is even written. This visual blueprinting directly prepares students for incremental development and helps them structure their future AP Create Tasks with clarity and confidence.

tasks: Map out a logical program flow using a standardized whiteboard diagram structure.

sessions.title: Incremental Development
sessions.description: Analyze why building software in small, manageable iterations reduces project risks and helps isolate bugs.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Start the session by drawing a stark contrast on the physical or virtual whiteboard: write 'The Big Bang Approach' on one side and 'The Incremental Approach' on the other. Use a non-software analogy that resonates universally, such as building a complex Lego castle. Explain that the Big Bang approach is like pouring all 5,000 pieces on the floor, ignoring the instruction booklet, attempting to assemble the entire castle in one massive sitting, and only checking if the pieces fit at the very end. If the foundation is slightly misaligned, the entire structure collapses. Contrast this with the Incremental Approach, where you build, test, and solidify the gateway, then the outer walls, and finally the towers, ensuring each section is fully stable before moving forward. This sets up the core intuition of the session: incremental development is not just a style of working, but a critical risk-management strategy in software engineering.

Now, translate this analogy directly into code-level logic on the whiteboard. Write out a conceptual timeline of two developers building a simple budgeting application. Developer A writes 500 lines of code across four features—inputting expenses, categorizing them, calculating totals, and generating a visual chart—without running the program even once. When they finally hit 'Run,' the console explodes with twenty interlocking syntax and logic errors. Developer B writes only the expense-inputting feature (50 lines), runs it, fixes one minor typo, verifies it works, and commits it. Only then do they write the calculation feature. Use this visualization to teach the fundamental rule of debugging: when you only change ten lines of code before testing, any new bug must exist within those ten lines. When you change five hundred lines, the bug could be anywhere, or worse, it could be an emergent issue caused by three different broken pieces interacting.

Introduce a common student misconception here: the belief that testing after every small change is a waste of time and slows down development. Address this head-on by drawing a graph of 'Time Spent vs. Project Complexity.' For non-iterative development, the curve is exponential; as the codebase grows, the time spent debugging skyrockets because of compounding errors. For incremental development, the curve is linear and predictable. Explain to the students that writing code incrementally actually saves massive amounts of time because it avoids 'integration hell'—the painful phase at the end of a project where independently written modules refuse to work together.

Transition into the comparative diagnostic case study practice. Present a scenario of a development team building an automated gradebook. Walk the students through a timeline where the team skipped intermediate testing and ended up with a bug where student averages are calculated as strings instead of numbers, causing a catastrophic failure in the final ranking algorithm. Have the students analyze this case study to identify the exact point where an incremental milestone (such as verifying the output data type of the calculation function before writing the sorting function) would have caught the error instantly. This analysis helps students develop the critical intuition required to plan their own development pipelines for the Create Task, ensuring they value progress in small, testable chunks over monolithic coding marathons.

tasks: Compare the incremental development model to a non-iterative model using a diagnostic case study.

sessions.title: Testing and Debugging
sessions.description: Learn systematically to design test cases, isolate errors, and use print statements or debugging tools to fix code issues.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Begin the session by addressing a fundamental truth of computer science: writing code that contains errors is not a sign of failure, but a natural step in the creative and logical process of software development. Frame debugging not as a frantic trial-and-error cycle, but as a systematic detective investigation. Introduce the goal of this session on the whiteboard: to transition from chaotic code-tinkering to structured diagnostic strategies. By treating programs as predictable state machines, students will learn to isolate precisely where and why a system diverges from its intended behavior.

Draw a clear line down the center of the whiteboard to categorize the two main types of bugs students will encounter on the AP exam and in their own projects: syntax errors and logic errors. Explain syntax errors as violations of the programming language's grammar rules, such as unmatched parentheses or misspelled keywords, which prevent the computer from translating or running the code. Contrast this with logic errors, where the code compiles and executes without crashing, but produces incorrect, unintended outputs because the underlying algorithm is flawed. Use a simple recipe analogy: a syntax error is like a recipe written in a language you do not speak, whereas a logic error is like successfully baking a cake but accidentally adding salt instead of sugar.

To make this concrete, write a short, buggy pseudocode snippet on the whiteboard representing a simple grade calculator or average-finder. Intentionally introduce a syntax error, such as a missing end-bracket, and a logic error, such as dividing the sum by a fixed number instead of the dynamic length of the list. Walk the students through the process of code tracing using a trace table. On the whiteboard, draw a grid tracking the values of each variable step-by-step through every line of code. This visual tracking demonstrates exactly how a logic error sneaks into the program execution and teaches students to distrust their assumptions about what the code does versus what it actually says.

Introduce systematic debugging strategies that move beyond mere guessing. Demonstrate the power of temporary print statements—sometimes called 'dirty debugging'—to output variable states at key milestones of the execution flow. Explain how this helps narrow down the search area when a program behaves unexpectedly. Transition this concept into professional toolsets, explaining how modern development environments use breakpoints to pause execution at specific lines, allowing programmers to inspect the 'live' memory state without polluting their source code with print statements.

Conclude the session by highlighting a major pitfall: the temptation to fix bugs by making random, unprincipled edits to the source code, which often introduces new, hidden errors. Emphasize that a developer must never change a line of code unless they can state a clear hypothesis about why that change will resolve the target issue. Guide the transition into the practice task where students will analyze a buggy code snippet, build their own trace tables, and categorize the discovered issues into syntax or logic errors, solidifying their analytical tracing skills before they begin writing complex programs of their own.

tasks: Trace a buggy snippet and identify logic errors versus syntax errors.

sessions.title: Feedback and Program Improvement
sessions.description: Explore how developers incorporate user testing data and code review feedback to optimize performance and user experience.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin the session by contextualizing the software development lifecycle. Students often believe that once code compiles and passes local tests, the project is finished. On the whiteboard, draw a circular feedback loop containing three nodes: Develop, Release, and Gather Feedback. Explain that user feedback is the ultimate reality check for software design. Without external perspectives, developers suffer from blind spots, overlooking unintuitive user interfaces or edge cases they didn't personally encounter. Emphasize that in the AP CSP framework, incorporating feedback is a formal requirement for refinement.

Draw a T-chart on the whiteboard to help students categorize incoming data. Label the left column 'Raw Tester Comment' and the right column 'Technical Action Item.' Explain that users do not speak in code; they report symptoms. A comment like 'the screen goes blank when I click too fast' is a raw symptom. Guide the students on how a developer translates this into a technical hypothesis, such as an unhandled race condition or rapid-fire events triggering multiple conflicting state changes. Contrast this with usability feedback, like 'I couldn't find the restart button,' which translates to an interface layout modification rather than a logical error. This distinction prevents developers from rewriting clean logic when simple layout updates are all that is needed.

Introduce a common industry framework for prioritizing feedback: Bugs versus Feature Requests. Detail how trying to implement every user suggestion leads to 'scope creep,' a fatal trap for student projects with fixed deadlines like the AP Create Task. Draw a prioritization grid on the board divided into Critical Bugs (blocks core functionality), Usability Fixes (impedes user path), and Aesthetic/Feature Requests (nice-to-have enhancements). Walk through how to aggressively prioritize critical bugs to ensure software stability before even considering aesthetic upgrades.

Engage the class in a structured walkthrough of a raw beta-tester feedback log. Present three specific comments on the board: 'The application crashed when I typed my name in the age box,' 'The red text is really hard to read against the black background,' and 'I want the game to save my progress online.' Guide the class to unpack each comment. For the first comment, demonstrate how to write a concrete debugging task: 'Add input validation to convert text input to integers and handle non-numeric strings without throwing an exception.' This process illustrates to students how vague frustration is converted into precise, systematic, and actionable code modifications.

tasks: Synthesize beta tester comments into actionable debugging tasks.

lectures.title: The Create Performance Task
lectures.description: Review the detailed criteria for the AP CSP Create Performance Task. Understand how to design, build, record, and document your personalized project reference.

sessions.title: Create Performance Task Requirements
sessions.description: Provide a comprehensive overview of the official College Board guidelines, deadlines, and scoring rubrics.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this session by demystifying the AP Computer Science Principles Create Performance Task, framing it not as a standard programming project, but as a highly structured portfolio submission that accounts for a significant portion of the student's AP score. The core concept to establish immediately is the strict alignment between the program code and the specific written response requirements. Many students fail to realize that a beautiful, complex game might receive a zero if it lacks the specific technical components mandated by the College Board rubric. On our whiteboard, we sketch the overarching architecture of the Create Task: the Program Code (which must contain student-developed lists and procedures), the Video (demonstrating execution), and the Personalized Project Reference, which is used during the end-of-course exam to answer written prompt questions. By laying out this three-part foundation first, we prevent the common misconception that the performance task is solely a coding assignment.

Next, we transition to an interactive whiteboard breakdown of the official scoring rubric, focusing heavily on what we call the 'non-negotiable technical targets.' We draw a grid mapping the key components: Data Abstraction (specifically, the creation and use of a list to manage program complexity), Procedural Abstraction (a student-developed procedure with at least one parameter that impacts execution), and Algorithm Implementation (which must include sequencing, selection, and iteration within that procedure). We emphasize to students that they must be the primary authors of these components. The pedagogical goal here is to shift their mindset from 'how do I build a cool app?' to 'how do I design an app that naturally incorporates a list and a parameter-driven procedure?' We explicitly point out that trivial or unused lists, or procedures without parameters, are the most frequent reasons students miss points on the rubric.

To solidify this rubric alignment, we introduce a matching practice exercise directly on the whiteboard. We present a list of realistic project activities—such as 'writing a function that takes a difficulty level and uses an if-statement and a loop to generate a quiz' or 'hardcoding ten separate variables instead of using an array to track high scores'—and ask students to match these activities to the corresponding rubric row or identify which row they violate. This interactive matching task is designed to reveal a crucial point of confusion: students often confuse visual complexity with logical abstraction. For instance, hardcoding ten variables might make a game look complete, but it completely fails the Data Abstraction rubric row because it does not use a list to manage complexity. Analyzing these candidate scenarios helps students internalize the strict criteria before they write a single line of code.

We wrap up the session by outlining the timeline and the strategic approach to documentation and recording. We discuss how the Create Task is no longer submitted as a static PDF response during the year, but rather how their code screenshots form the 'Personalized Project Reference' that they will directly reference during the AP Exam's written response section. We draw a timeline of checkpoints, stressing that the video demonstration must be unedited and showcase the core functionality, including the inputs and outputs that involve the list and procedure. This final structural overview ensures students leave the session with a clear roadmap, understanding that clean documentation and compliance with the rubric constraints are their primary pathways to a high score.

tasks: Match candidate project activities to corresponding rows of the AP Create Task rubric.

sessions.title: Choosing an Appropriate Project
sessions.description: Learn how to select a project idea that is achievable yet fully meets the technical parameters of the AP assessment.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Begin the session by framing the project selection process as the single most critical decision of the Create Performance Task. Instructors should emphasize that many students run into a classic trap: they choose a project based on visual flashiness rather than programmatic utility. On the physical or virtual whiteboard, draw a clear distinction between a 'cool app' and an 'AP-compliant app.' Explain that the College Board does not award points for complex graphics or user interface design; instead, points are earned strictly through functional code architecture, specifically involving data abstraction and procedural complexity. This opening hook is designed to shift the student's mindset from game designer to systems architect.

Next, lay out the 'AP Checklist' on the board in two high-visibility columns. The left column must outline the Data Abstraction requirement: a student-defined list that is actively used to manage complexity in the program, meaning that without this list, the code would become significantly harder to write or maintain. The right column must outline the Procedural Abstraction requirement: a student-developed procedure with at least one parameter, containing sequencing, selection (conditionals), and iteration (loops) that directly affects the behavior of the program. Address a common student misconception here: many believe that any list or procedure will do, but point out that 'tacked-on' lists (like a list of three elements that are never looped through) will result in zero points on the official rubric. Explain how these two pillars form the scaffolding of their entire submission.

Introduce the evaluation exercise by presenting three distinct student project concepts on the whiteboard. Case A is a visually stunning physics-based puzzle game that relies on custom coordinate math but uses no arrays or loops. Case B is a basic clicker game that updates a single global score variable but contains no lists or custom functions. Case C is a simplified vocabulary practice system that stores terms and definitions in lists, uses a parameter-driven function to filter words by difficulty level, and loops through the selected items to generate quiz questions. Walk through each scenario, showing how to test them against the two-column checklist. Detail how Case C, despite having the simplest interface, is the only option that naturally and elegantly satisfies every rubric requirement.

Conclude the whiteboard session by mapping out the decision-making framework students must use when brainstormed concepts are put to the test. Instructors should model how to ask critical questions about their own ideas: 'Where will my loop go?' and 'How does my list make my code shorter or more modular?' Have students analyze the three sample ideas from the practice task, helping them identify the operational flaws in the first two options and teaching them to recognize the structured logic of the winning choice. This systematic evaluation prevents students from committing to a project that would force them to rewrite their code weeks before the AP deadline.

tasks: Evaluate three project ideas and select the one that best supports the required list and procedure components.

sessions.title: Developing the Program Code
sessions.description: Review strategies for structuring your code cleanly while keeping track of development milestones.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this session by addressing a classic software engineering pitfall that derails many AP Create Tasks: the 'all-at-once' coding trap. Many students believe they should write their entire program from start to finish before running it for the first time. On the whiteboard, draw a contrasting timeline showing this monolithic approach versus an incremental development approach. Explain that the College Board actively looks for evidence of an iterative process where programs are written, tested, and refined in small, manageable pieces. This session focuses on establishing a concrete development timeline that guarantees students have functional, testable code at every step of their journey, specifically isolating the complex list and procedure requirements.

Next, lay out the concept of a modular milestone blueprint on the board. The first milestone must always be setting up the basic user interface or input/output skeleton. We call this 'stubbing.' If a student is building a fitness tracker, they should first ensure a simple button-click outputs a placeholder message to the screen before writing any calculations. Explain the logical chain here: if your input mechanisms are faulty, you cannot accurately test your lists or loops. By validating user input and basic output first, students establish a stable foundation, completely eliminating UI bugs from the equation before they move on to core data structures.

Once the basic interface is validated, we move to the next logical milestone on our timeline: Data Abstraction integration. On the whiteboard, write 'Milestone 2: The List Sandbox.' Explain to the students that they should write the code to initialize their list and practice adding, removing, or displaying items in their simplest forms. A major student misconception here is attempting to loop through or filter a list before verifying that the list actually stores data correctly. Instruct teachers to demonstrate how to use simple print statements or console logs to output the raw state of the list after each operation. If the console does not show the data growing or changing, they must not write any more complex code. This clean separation of concerns prevents massive debugging headaches later.

With a working list, students are ready to introduce their procedural logic—the algorithms that contain selection (conditionals) and iteration (loops). Draw a flowchart showing how data flows from the list, through a custom procedure, and back to the user interface. Emphasize that Milestone 3 involves testing this algorithm with boundary cases. For example, if a loop is supposed to search a list for matching elements, what happens if the list is empty? What happens if every single item matches? Teach students to intentionally create test cases for these scenarios. If the procedure fails on an empty list, they can patch the bug immediately rather than wondering if the issue lies in their UI, their list initialization, or their loop logic.

To wrap up the conceptual lecture, transition to the interactive design phase. Ask students to draft their personal development timeline on paper or a digital canvas, explicitly detailing where they will place their testing checkpoints. The core of this practice is forcing them to articulate exactly how they will verify that their list works before they write their loop, and how they will test their loop before they film their final video. By building this self-reflection into their timeline, students learn to treat debugging as an ongoing, predictable activity rather than an emergency measure, fully preparing them to write the required development narrative in the written responses.

tasks: Outline a personal development timeline with checkpoints for testing lists and loops.

sessions.title: Recording the Program Video
sessions.description: Understand the visual and technical specifications for filming your program's live run to prove its functionality.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this session by addressing the core purpose of the Create Performance Task program video: it is the primary visual proof that the student's code actually works and executes the claimed functionality. Students often mistake this for a marketing video or a highly edited tutorial, which can result in a score of zero if the examiners suspect artificial cuts or falsified execution. The teacher must clarify that this video must show one continuous, unedited run of the program demonstrating input, program functionality (processing), and output. To build early intuition, we sketch a 'flow of interaction' diagram on the board: User Action (Input) -> System Logic (Processing) -> Screen Update (Output). This diagram serves as a visual checklist for what the recording must capture.

Next, we break down the strict technical specifications mandated by the College Board. The video must be under 1 minute in length and less than 30 megabytes in size, saved in a common format like MP4, WebM, or AVI. Because of these constraints, students often run into the pitfall of recording a massive high-resolution screen capture that fails the size upload limit, or they try to rush through the demo and miss showing key functionality. The teacher should model how to configure basic screen recording software to capture only the active application window rather than the entire desktop, and suggest lower frame rates (like 15 or 30 fps) or standard resolutions (like 720p) to keep the file size minimal while maintaining readability of any on-screen text.

We then transition to the core practice activity: assessing a sample video draft that has been deliberately designed with common issues. The teacher displays a checklist on the board: 'Is there an unedited cut?', 'Is user input clearly visible (e.g., typing, mouse clicks)?', and 'Does the output directly reflect that input?'. In this interactive walkthrough, the teacher points out how a student might show a maze game but cut the video right before the player hits the goal block to save time. This is a critical error; the teacher must emphasize that any visible editing cut disqualifies the video from proving the code's true execution. The practice task guides students to spot these cuts, identify missing input actions (like a mouse click that isn't highlighted or explained), and ensure the final output state is clearly readable on screen for at least a couple of seconds.

To wrap up, we address how to handle programs that do not have a traditional graphical user interface, such as command-line programs or audio-based applications. If a program uses console input and output, the video must clearly show the terminal prompts and the user typing responses. If the program generates audio output, the student must ensure that system audio is captured in the recording rather than just room microphone noise. The teacher concludes by prompting students to plan their recording sequence beforehand by writing a quick three-step storyboard: what input they will provide, what logic it triggers, and how the success state will be visually verified.

tasks: Assess a sample video draft to confirm it displays user inputs, actions, and output results without editing cuts.

sessions.title: Documenting Data Abstraction
sessions.description: Learn how to capture and explain code blocks that use a list to manage complexity in your program.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this session by addressing the core concept of data abstraction on the physical whiteboard. Draw a single, unified variable box labeled 'studentScores' with multiple indexed slots, and contrast it with a chaotic swarm of individual variables labeled 'score1', 'score2', 'score3', up to 'score100'. This visualization immediately establishes the foundational intuition of why lists exist. Teachers should emphasize that data abstraction is not just about holding multiple values, but about grouping related data under one identifier to simplify program logic, which directly addresses the AP CSP 'managing complexity' requirement. This setup prepares students to understand the architectural difference between a program that scales dynamically and one that breaks under minor updates.

Next, we pivot to the specific requirements of the AP CSP Written Response regarding data abstraction. Detail the two mandatory code segments students must identify: one showing how data is loaded or stored in the list, and another showing how that list is actually used to achieve the program's purpose. A common pitfall here is that students often submit a list that is declared but never dynamically traversed or modified. Explain to teachers how to guide students to write code where the list's size is not hardcoded, pointing out that using a loop to process a list of variable length is the gold standard for proving that the list genuinely manages complexity.

We then walk through the process of drafting the written justification. The teacher should model writing a clear, evidence-based response using a mock 'grocery inventory tracker' project. On the whiteboard, map out the logical chain: identify the list name, explain what the data represents, state how the list manages complexity, and finally, explicitly describe the 'counterfactual'—what the code would look like without the list. The teacher should write out the bad counterfactual ('I would need 100 variables') and refine it into a high-scoring response ('Without the list, I would need separate variables for each item, requiring 100 individual conditional blocks instead of a single, scalable loop, making the codebase highly prone to bugs and impossible to expand').

Finally, transition into the hands-on practice block where students draft their own written justification based on a provided scenario. The teacher should circulate the room, actively looking for vague language like 'the list makes my code shorter' or 'it is easier to read.' Instruct teachers to push students to specify the algorithmic cost: without the list, every single variable would require manual, duplicated logic blocks for processing, rendering features like sorting or filtering practically impossible to maintain. Review these drafts on the board by annotating student responses live, highlighting where they successfully linked the list structure to maintenance efficiency.

tasks: Draft a written response explaining how a specific list manages complexity and why an alternative would be harder to maintain.

sessions.title: Documenting Procedural Abstraction
sessions.description: Understand how to select, document, and explain a student-developed procedure containing parameters and logic.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this session by addressing the core concept of procedural abstraction on the virtual whiteboard, defining it not just as a container for code, but as a deliberate design choice that simplifies program complexity. For the AP Create Performance Task, students must develop a procedure that contains at least one parameter that impacts its execution, and they must explain how this procedure works. The teacher should sketch a simple analogy on the board: imagine a 'smart microwave' button. Instead of having separate buttons for heating 1 cup of soup, 2 cups of soup, or a plate of pasta, we have a single generalized 'Heat' button that accepts two inputs—the type of food and the portion size. These inputs are our parameters, which allow a single block of logic to adapt dynamically to different situations. This analogy immediately establishes why procedural abstraction is useful: it prevents code repetition and makes the overall program easier to maintain.

Next, the teacher will visually separate the concept of a parameter (the variable placeholder defined in the procedure's header) from an argument (the actual value passed into the procedure during a specific call). A common pitfall for students is confusing these two terms or failing to show how the parameter actually dictates different execution paths within the procedure. On the whiteboard, draw a clear, language-neutral function header like `procedure calculateScore(points, multiplier)`. The teacher will trace how `points` and `multiplier` act as local variables inside the function body, pointing out that their values are not hardcoded but depend entirely on what the caller provides. To address the rubric requirements, the teacher must demonstrate that the procedure cannot simply be a passive sequence of steps; it must use the parameter in some conditional logic (selection) or loop (iteration) to dynamically change what the program does based on that input.

To bridge this theory with the required written response, the teacher will write a sample, flawed student response on the board and guide the class through a critique. For example, a student might write: 'My parameter is x, and it makes my program run by changing the score.' The teacher should explain why this is insufficient—it lacks specificity and fails to describe the direct causal relationship between the parameter's value and the path of code execution. The teacher will then model a high-scoring response: 'The parameter `userLevel` determines which threshold score the program uses to evaluate performance. If `userLevel` is equal to "expert", the program executes the branching logic that checks if the score is above 90; otherwise, it checks if the score is above 70. This directly alters the output displayed to the user.' This walkthrough teaches students how to write with precision, focusing on the cause-and-effect relationship between parameter input and conditional branching.

Finally, the teacher will initiate an interactive drafting exercise. Students will be presented with a dummy code block containing a procedure with a parameter and must write a short, three-sentence draft explaining: (1) what the parameter is, (2) how its value changes the flow of control inside the procedure, and (3) what result is returned or displayed as a consequence. The teacher will circulate to catch a critical misconception: students selecting a procedure that has parameters but where the parameter is never actually used inside the body, or where the parameter's value does not change the logic path. By diagnosing and correcting these dry runs in real-time, students build the exact analytical skills needed to confidently document their own procedural abstractions for their portfolio submission.

tasks: Draft a response identifying a procedure's parameter and its effect on the code execution.

sessions.title: Documenting the Student-Developed Algorithm
sessions.description: Learn how to detail the specific algorithm inside your procedure, illustrating sequencing, selection, and iteration.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this session by addressing a central pillar of the AP CSP Create Performance Task: the requirement that students develop and document an algorithm that contains sequencing, selection, and iteration. Many students stumble here because they confuse a basic sequence of instructions with a structurally complex algorithm. The core pedagogical goal of this whiteboard session is to clarify exactly how these three components—sequencing (the chronological flow of steps), selection (conditional statements like 'if-else'), and iteration (loops like 'for' or 'while')—must fit together inside a single student-developed procedure. Our first visual on the whiteboard will be a clear architectural blueprint showing a nested procedure to help students conceptualize these relationships visually rather than just memorizing definitions.

To bridge the gap for students who benefit from a concept-first, public-lecture approach, we will construct a mock Python/JavaScript hybrid pseudocode block on the whiteboard. This block will represent a high-level real-world scenario, such as a function called `updateScores(scoreList)` that filters high scores, calculates bonuses, and modifies values. By tracing the execution of this code block step-by-step, we demonstrate how sequencing exists in the sequential assignment of variables at the start, how selection is introduced when we check if a score exceeds a threshold, and how iteration is achieved as we loop through the list to analyze each individual score. This visual mapping prevents the common pitfall where students write three disconnected blocks of code; we must emphasize that selection and iteration must work *within* the sequential flow of the same major procedure.

Next, the lesson pivots to demonstrating how to explicitly document this algorithm for the AP readers. We show how to highlight the exact code lines that perform each function and how to translate code logic into plain English for the written response templates. A common misconception we must proactively dismantle is the belief that 'selection' simply means using any 'if' statement; we need to explain that the AP rubric requires this selection to actively determine the branch of execution that directly affects the program's ultimate output. The whiteboard breakdown will map out a flowchart alongside the code snippet to illustrate how a single change in the input data alters the path through the selection statement and changes the loop's behavior.

We wrap up the session with an active identification exercise. We present a new, unannotated code block on the whiteboard and challenge students to trace and label where sequencing ends, where iteration begins, and where selection nests within that iteration. This practice is designed to reveal whether students can isolate these elements structurally or if they are still treating their code as an undifferentiated wall of text. By verifying their understanding on the whiteboard, we ensure they are fully prepared to select, isolate, and document their own algorithms when they compile their Personalized Project Reference.

tasks: Identify where sequencing, selection, and iteration appear within a sample function block.

sessions.title: Preparing for the Written Responses
sessions.description: Formulate solid strategies for the end-of-course written responses using your Personalized Project Reference.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin by setting the stage for the written portion of the AP Computer Science Principles exam, demystifying how the Personalized Project Reference is utilized on exam day. On the left side of the whiteboard, draw a mock-up of the official reference sheet containing only raw, uncommented code blocks, and on the right, draw the AP Exam booklet containing open-ended prompts. It is vital to emphasize to students that they will not be writing new code from scratch during this exam section; instead, they are performing a high-stakes, analytical post-mortem on their own pre-submitted work. This conceptual framing helps alleviate anxiety, pivoting their mindset from creative programming to rigorous, evidence-based technical writing.

Next, we introduce a dummy project on the whiteboard to serve as our anchor illustration: a simplified 'Smart Thermostat' program. On the board, write out a clean, text-based list named `dailyTemps` and a procedure named `analyzeWeather(tempList, threshold)` that iterates through the list, filters values above the threshold, and returns an alert level. By using a highly intuitive physical world example, we ensure that students of all backgrounds can immediately grasp the program's logic before we layer on the complex, multi-part questions typical of the AP Exam. We walk through how the dummy list represents data abstraction and how the procedure embodies procedural abstraction.

With our dummy code on the board, we simulate the first major category of exam questions: Data Abstraction analysis. The teacher writes a sample prompt asking how the list manages complexity and what would happen if it were removed. Here, we address a massive student pitfall: writing vague, hand-waving responses like 'the list makes it easier' or simply repeating the prompt. Instead, we model a structured, two-part response strategy. First, state what the list holds and how it is processed collectively. Second, contrast this with the nightmare alternative: declaring fifty individual variables (`temp1`, `temp2`, etc.) and writing fifty separate conditional statements, showing that the code would become practically unmaintainable.

We then transition to the Procedural Abstraction prompt, which is often the most technically demanding portion of the exam. On the whiteboard, we map out the relationship between 'parameters' (the placeholders inside the function definition) and 'arguments' (the actual values passed during a call). We construct a diagnostic table where we trace two distinct execution paths through our `analyzeWeather` function using different arguments—for example, passing a list that triggers the threshold versus one that does not. The teacher demonstrates how to write a precise, step-by-step trace that identifies which branches of the conditional statement are executed and what specific values are returned, training students to avoid the common mistake of explaining the code generally rather than tracing a specific path.

To cement these concepts, we transition to an active whiteboard practice moment. The teacher presents a new, slightly modified dummy code block—such as an automated 'Inventory Alert' system—and tasks the class with drafting an analysis of its core algorithm. As students construct their responses, the teacher moves around the room, specifically checking to see if they can point out where sequencing, selection, and iteration explicitly interact within the procedure. We highlight a final critical pitfall: students often describe these three algorithmic elements in isolation rather than explaining how they work together to achieve the procedure's overall goal. We conclude by summarizing the core writing templates that students should memorize to ensure their exam-day responses are clear, technically accurate, and fully aligned with the College Board's scoring rubric.

tasks: Analyze a set of sample exam questions based on a dummy project reference and practice writing clear, evidence-based answers.
