units.description: Learn the logical and syntax frameworks of computer programming. This unit starts with fundamental variables, moves to execution flows (sequencing, selection, iteration), and concludes with procedural abstraction and algorithm complexity.

lectures.title: Programming Fundamentals
lectures.description: Begin writing code. Explore program statements, input/output structures, variables, arithmetic operators, and random generators.

sessions.title: Program Statements
sessions.description: Explain how computer programs run sequential lines of instructions from top to bottom.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Welcome students to the logical core of AP Computer Science Principles. As we begin our journey into programming, we must first demystify how a computer reads and executes code. The fundamental concept of this session is the sequential execution model. We will represent this on the whiteboard as an assembly line or a single-track train route: a CPU processes a program one statement at a time, strictly from top to bottom. It is crucial to establish this intuition early because human brains naturally try to read entire pages of code at once, looking for patterns, whereas computers are stubbornly literal, line-by-line machines.

Draw a three-line sequence on the whiteboard. Explain that a 'statement' is a complete instruction that commands the computer to perform a specific action. Emphasize that execution flow starts at line one, fully completes it, and only then steps down to line two. A common rookie mistake is assuming that later lines can retroactively change the execution of earlier lines, or that lines run simultaneously. By mapping the execution process onto a vertical arrow pointing downwards alongside our block of code, we physically demonstrate the chronological flow of computational time.

Next, introduce a simple terminal trace on the board. We will write a three-line sequential pseudo-script. Explain to the students how the console or terminal acts as our output canvas. As we dry-run this script line-by-line, we will draw a 'terminal output window' on the side of the whiteboard. We physically write down each character or message as it is processed by the statement. This exercise teaches students to separate the source code (the instructions) from the runtime state (the actual output generated over time).

To wrap up, engage the class in a collaborative tracing exercise. Give them a new 3-line script on the board and ask them to predict the final output of the terminal window. Look out for students who skip lines or misinterpret the sequence of execution. This quick practice moment reveals whether they have internalized the strict top-to-bottom paradigm or are still trying to read the block of code as a single holistic paragraph. Clear up any confusion by stepping through the execution path one final time with a bright colored marker.

tasks: Trace the terminal output of a simple 3-line sequential program script.

sessions.title: Inputs and Outputs
sessions.description: Examine how programs receive outside data and output processed text, values, or visual indications.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this session by addressing the core relationship between a program and the physical world: Inputs and Outputs (I/O). Because our learner has requested a concept-first public lecture style, we will introduce this using the intuitive metaphor of a black box processor. On the whiteboard, draw a large central box labeled 'Program / Process'. Draw an incoming arrow on the left side labeled 'Input' and an outgoing arrow on the right side labeled 'Output'. Emphasize that programs do not run in a vacuum; they exist to transform raw external data into useful results. This visual anchor establishes that inputs are how a system senses its environment (such as a keypress, a sensor reading, or a mouse click), while outputs are how the system acts upon or communicates with that environment (such as rendering text on a screen, sounding an alarm, or spinning a physical motor).

To unpack the input process, draw a keyboard and a mouse feeding into the input arrow. Explain that raw inputs arrive at the computer as electrical signals, which the operating system translates into characters or coordinates before our program can even see them. A common student misconception here is confusing the hardware device (the keyboard) with the actual data value the program receives (the string character, like 'A'). Explain that when a user presses a key, the program captures this event as an input stream. On the board, write out a conceptual function signature like `getUserInput()` and illustrate how this function 'listens' to the hardware buffer, temporarily pausing execution until data is available, and then hands that data over to our variables for processing.

Next, shift the focus to the output process. Extend the outgoing arrow on the whiteboard toward a sketch of a monitor screen. Introduce the concept of the standard output stream, typically represented as a terminal console or a graphical display interface. Walk the students through how a program takes internally processed data (such as a numerical calculation or a concatenated string) and formats it into human-readable characters. Emphasize that output is not just about printing text to a terminal; visual elements, sound waves, and saved file structures are all forms of program output. This is a crucial conceptual link: inputs feed the program's logic, and outputs justify that logic by delivering a tangible result.

For the interactive practice, guide the students to sketch a conceptual pipeline representing how a search bar processes input to produce a display string. On their own whiteboards, students should draw three distinct zones: the Input zone (representing a user typing the search query), the Process zone (where a conceptual function appends a greeting or formats the query), and the Output zone (where the stylized text is rendered on the UI). This exercise is designed to reveal whether students can trace the conversion of physical keystrokes into clean, processed textual data. Address the common trap of forgetting that the program must store and format the text before rendering it, reinforcing that what goes in must be handled programmatically before it can come out.

tasks: Sketch a model illustrating how a software function processes a keyboard input into a display string.

sessions.title: Variables and Assignment
sessions.description: Master how computers store data in named memory containers using the assignment operator.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Welcome back, class. Today, we are diving into one of the most fundamental concepts in all of computer science: variables and the assignment operator. I want you to imagine a row of physical lockers lined up along our classroom wall. Each locker has a unique label on the outside—like 'score', 'username', or 'temp'—and inside, there is room to hold exactly one piece of paper containing a single value. This physical metaphor is critical because it helps dispel a massive early programming misconception: that a variable is like an algebraic equation. In math, 'x = y + 5' is a statement of permanent equality. In computer science, however, the assignment operator is an active instruction—a command to 'go fetch a value, calculate it, and stuff it into this specific locker, throwing away whatever was previously inside.'

Let's sketch this concept on the whiteboard. Draw a neat box and label it 'points'. Inside the box, write the number 10. This represents our initial state: `points ← 10` (using the standard AP CSP pseudocode arrow). Now, right below it, write the instruction `points ← 15`. Ask the students: what happens to the 10? Explicitly point out that the 10 does not sit next to the 15, and they do not add together. The old value of 10 is completely destroyed, overwritten by the incoming 15. This is the 'destructive' nature of variable assignment. Emphasize that the left side of the assignment arrow or equals sign is always the *destination* (the name of the container), while the right side is the *source* or the expression to be evaluated. Students frequently write things like `10 = x` because they are thinking like mathematicians; we must proactively correct this by tracing the direction of data flow from right to left.

Now, let's step up the complexity and look at sequential dependency with variables referencing other variables. Write three lines on the board: 
Line 1: `a ← 5` 
Line 2: `b ← a` 
Line 3: `a ← 12` 
Ask the class: 'At the end of these three lines, what is the value stored in container b?' Pause and let them look. A common rookie mistake is to assume that because `b` was set to `a` on Line 2, `b` acts as a shortcut link that dynamically changes whenever `a` changes. They might incorrectly guess that `b` is now 12. Walk them through the state step-by-step to show why this is false: on Line 2, the computer looks at the locker labeled `a`, reads the value inside (which is 5), and copies that *value* into `b`. Locker `b` now holds its own independent copy of the number 5. When Line 3 updates `a` to 12, locker `b` remains untouched. Building this sequential tracing habit is the absolute key to success on the AP Exam's pseudocode questions.

To solidify this, let us move to a practical dry-run challenge on the board. Write down a classic variable-swapping algorithm block: 
`x ← 10` 
`y ← 20` 
`temp ← x` 
`x ← y` 
`y ← temp` 
Ask students to draw a state table on their scratch paper with three columns: `x`, `y`, and `temp`. Have them trace each line execution by execution, updating the numbers in their columns. This exercise is designed to reveal whether they understand why a third 'temporary' variable is necessary to swap two values without losing data. If we simply wrote `x ← y` and then `y ← x`, both would end up holding 20, and the original value of `x` would be lost forever. Point out this logical pitfall and celebrate the elegant utility of the temporary container. This visual trace converts an abstract programming trick into an unforgettable logical milestone.

tasks: Trace variables in a block of assignments where variable values overwrite previous ones.

sessions.title: Data Types
sessions.description: Differentiate primitive structures like integers, floats, strings, and booleans, noting how memory models categorize them.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this session by addressing a fundamental concept: how computers organize and label different kinds of information in memory. In a whiteboard lecture style, we introduce the concept of 'Data Types' as logical buckets or labels that tell the computer how to interpret the underlying 1s and 0s. Without a data type, a sequence of bits in memory is just raw noise; with a data type, it becomes a number we can add, a word we can read, or a state we can check. 

We sketch a series of boxes on the whiteboard representing memory locations, and label each with a variable name alongside its designated data type. First, we introduce integers (whole numbers like 15, -4, 0) and explain that they are used for countable, exact quantities. We contrast this immediately with floats (floating-point real numbers containing decimals, like 19.99 or -0.5), pointing out that floats allow for precision but can introduce round-off errors because computers cannot represent every infinite decimal perfectly in binary. 

Next, we introduce strings, which are sequences of text characters enclosed in quotation marks, like "123 Main St" or "hello". A common point of confusion for students is mistaking a string containing digits, such as "42", for an actual mathematical integer. We highlight this critical misconception on the board: you can add 5 to the integer 42 to get 47, but trying to add 5 to the string "42" will either cause an error or result in text glueing ("425"), depending on the programming language. We then introduce Booleans, which store exactly one of two values: true or false. We explain that Booleans act as simple logical light switches, which will become the foundation of our upcoming decision-making blocks.

To solidify this taxonomy, we pivot to an interactive whiteboard sorting exercise. We draw a table with four columns labeled Integer, Float, String, and Boolean, and write four realistic data fields on the side: 'age', 'price', 'address', and 'loginStatus'. We guide students through assigning each field to its optimal type: 'age' maps to an Integer because it represents whole years; 'price' maps to a Float to handle cents; 'address' must be a String because it contains spaces and letters; and 'loginStatus' maps perfectly to a Boolean (true for logged in, false for logged out). By dry-running this classification, we reveal the design decisions developers must make before they ever write their first line of code.

tasks: Assign correct storage types to fields such as age, price, address, and loginStatus.

sessions.title: Expressions and Operators
sessions.description: Formulate mathematical expressions using standard arithmetic and modulus operators.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this whiteboard session by establishing the concept of an expression as a recipe for a single value. After covering basic variables, students must now understand how computers perform calculations. Draw a parallel between standard algebraic notation and computer science syntax. Explain that while standard math is often descriptive, programming expressions are active instructions that must resolve to a single concrete value before that value can be stored or used. Walk through the standard arithmetic operators (+, -, *, /) on the board, pointing out that multiplication and division symbols differ from school math to accommodate standard keyboard keys. 

Introduce the order of operations, emphasizing that computers strictly follow PEMDAS/BODMAS rules. To illustrate this logic chain, write an expression like 'result = 5 + 3 * 2' on the whiteboard. Explain how the computer first identifies the multiplication operator, resolves '3 * 2' to 6, and only then performs the addition to get 11. Contrast this with the common student misconception that expressions are evaluated strictly from left to right, which would incorrectly yield 16. Show how adding parentheses 'result = (5 + 3) * 2' alters the sequence of evaluation. This visual breakdown helps students build a mental interpreter, preventing syntax and logic errors in complex code lines.

Next, introduce the modulus operator (MOD or %), which is often the most unfamiliar operator for beginners. Define it conceptually as the 'remainder locator' rather than a standard division tool. On the board, write out the long division of 17 divided by 5. Circle the quotient (3) and highlight the remainder (2). Show that while '17 / 5' might yield a decimal like 3.4 depending on the language, '17 MOD 5' strictly evaluates to 2. Explain why this operation is incredibly powerful in computer science: it helps determine even or odd numbers (x MOD 2), manage cyclical patterns like clock hours (time MOD 12), and wrap grid coordinates in game boundaries.

Transition to the hands-on practice phase to solidify these rules. Present students with the composite mathematical statements involving addition, division, and modulo operations, such as '12 + 8 MOD 3' and '(14 + 6) / 5 MOD 2'. Have them compute the outputs step-by-step on their own scratchpads. As they work, watch for students who try to apply MOD before parentheses or who confuse the quotient of a division with the remainder of a modulo operation. Use their written steps to diagnose whether they are misinterpreting operator precedence or failing to carry out integer remainder math correctly. Conclude by summarizing how these fundamental operators serve as the mathematical engine for any advanced algorithms they will build later in the unit.

tasks: Compute outputs for mathematical statements involving addition, division, and modulo operations.

sessions.title: Random Values
sessions.description: Understand how to generate pseudorandom ranges to introduce unpredictable behaviors into games or simulations.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this session by introducing randomness as the foundational driver of unpredictability in software, moving away from deterministic state changes. The primary concept here is the pseudorandom number generator, which simulates true randomness within fixed bounds. To make this concrete, we draw a visual boundary on the whiteboard representing a 'range envelope.' Explain that computers need strict boundaries to function; thus, an unconstrained random number is useless. We introduce the AP CSP pseudocode standard `RANDOM(a, b)` where both `a` and `b` are inclusive. On the board, write `RANDOM(1, 5)` and trace its potential outputs—1, 2, 3, 4, or 5. A common student pitfall is assuming that the upper bound is exclusive (like in Python's `randrange`), so we must explicitly write 'inclusive' next to our boundaries on the board and highlight that every integer within the range has an equal probability of being selected.

Once students understand the basic generator, we transition to scaling and shifting these outputs using basic arithmetic. This is where mathematical operations meet logic. We write the expression `RANDOM(1, 10) * 2` on the board. Instead of just giving the answer, guide students through a two-step transformation model. Step one is evaluating the core generator: what are the absolute minimum and maximum values that `RANDOM(1, 10)` can produce? Write down 1 and 10 as the extreme anchors. Step two is applying the multiplier: we multiply both the minimum and maximum by 2, yielding 2 and 20. But we must warn students of a critical logical trap here: this expression does *not* generate all integers between 2 and 20. Because the generator only yields integers {1, 2, 3, ..., 10} and then multiplies each by 2, the output set consists strictly of even numbers {2, 4, 6, 8, ..., 20}.

To solidify this distinction, contrast `RANDOM(1, 10) * 2` with `RANDOM(2, 20)`. On the whiteboard, draw two parallel number lines. For `RANDOM(2, 20)`, shade every single integer point from 2 to 20, representing 19 possible outcomes. For `RANDOM(1, 10) * 2`, place dots only on the even integer marks, showing only 10 possible outcomes. This visual juxtaposition immediately resolves the misconception that multiplying a random range simply expands the continuous integer span. Explain that scaling changes the step size between possible outcomes, whereas adding a constant—such as `RANDOM(1, 10) + 5`—shifts the entire continuous block of numbers upward.

We conclude with a brief, interactive whiteboard tracing task. Ask students to evaluate an expression like `RANDOM(0, 4) * 3 + 1`. Walk through the execution order: first evaluate the random range [0, 4], then scale by multiplying by 3 to get the intermediate set {0, 3, 6, 9, 12}, and finally shift by adding 1 to arrive at the final set of possible values {1, 4, 7, 10, 13}. This step-by-step unpacking ensures students can confidently decode any nested random expression they encounter on the AP exam.

tasks: Determine the range of possible outcomes from an expression such as RANDOM(1, 10) * 2.

lectures.title: Algorithms and Control Structures
lectures.description: Learn to write complex algorithms. This lecture uses standard AP pseudocode to explore Boolean decisions, conditionals, and loops.

sessions.title: Algorithms and Pseudocode
sessions.description: Define what makes an algorithm, and learn to write your solutions in a language-agnostic pseudocode format.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this foundational session of Unit 3 by defining what an algorithm actually is from a concept-first perspective, catering directly to learners who benefit from intuitive, non-technical entry points. Introduce the core definition of an algorithm as a precise, step-by-step set of instructions designed to accomplish a specific task or solve a problem. It is essential to emphasize that algorithms exist independently of any computer programming language. To anchor this, use a physical analogy on the virtual whiteboard: a culinary recipe. If the instructions say 'bake until done' or 'add a pinch of salt,' they are too ambiguous for a computer. Explain that a true algorithm requires absolute clarity, a finite number of steps, and must eventually terminate. This concept-first framing prevents the common misconception that programming is just memorizing syntax, highlighting instead that computer science is fundamentally about logical problem-solving.

Transitioning from the abstract idea of an algorithm to a structured representation, introduce the concept of pseudocode. Explain that pseudocode is an informal, high-level description of a computer program written in a blend of natural language and simplified code-like structures. It is language-agnostic, meaning it is not restricted by the strict, finicky syntax rules of Python, Java, or JavaScript, yet it provides enough structure to be easily translated into any of them. Sketch a simple side-by-side comparison on the whiteboard showing a task described in messy natural language, structured pseudocode, and then actual code. Demonstrate how pseudocode acts as the crucial planning bridge, stripping away syntax anxiety so the programmer can focus entirely on the logical flow.

Now, introduce the three fundamental building blocks of all algorithms: sequencing, selection, and iteration. Even though we will dive deeper into these in upcoming sessions, providing a high-level preview here is critical for logical continuity. Use the whiteboard to draw a simple flowchart or block diagram showing how sequencing is just a linear stack of steps, selection is a fork in the road based on a decision, and iteration is a loop that repeats. Explain that no matter how complex a modern software system or AI model is, it is ultimately constructed from these same three basic structures. This overview demystifies programming, showing students that complex logic is built from simple, understandable components.

To cement these concepts, guide the class through an interactive modeling exercise: writing pseudocode for a real-world task, such as preparing a cup of coffee. On the whiteboard, start with a highly ambiguous, naive set of instructions like 'boil water, put coffee in cup, pour water.' Then, prompt the students to find the logical gaps. What if there is no mug? What if the water is already hot? Redraft the steps systematically into structured, indented blocks. Address the common trap where students write overly vague steps (like 'make coffee') or get bogged down in unnecessary micro-details. Show how to strike the right balance of precision using clear action verbs and logical grouping. This exercise prepares them for the practice task, demonstrating how to break a familiar, automated physical routine down into unambiguous, executable logical blocks.

tasks: Express a real-world task like making coffee in structured pseudocode blocks.

sessions.title: Sequencing
sessions.description: Understand execution sequencing, where line-by-line order dictates calculations and results.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this session by introducing sequencing as the fundamental heartbeat of all computing programs. In line-by-line execution, the precise ordering of operations is not merely a stylistic choice; it changes the final state of memory itself. To set a concept-first, approachable tone, the instructor should write three simple operations on the board: setting a variable, adding to it, and printing it. By switching the print statement with the addition statement, we visually demonstrate how an identical set of instructions yielding a different output when rearranged. This establishes the critical rule of sequencing: code executes sequentially from top to bottom, and computers have no foresight of upcoming lines. They only act on the current state of variables.

Next, we transition to a standard AP pseudocode context. The major conceptual pitfall for learners here is treating the assignment arrow (←) or equal sign as an algebraic equation rather than an active, unidirectional data copy. Students often assume that if we write `y ← x`, any subsequent change to `x` will automatically update `y`. To pre-empt this common misconception, the instructor will draw 'memory boxes' on the whiteboard. By tracing `x ← 5`, then `y ← x`, and finally `x ← 10`, we visually show that the value in `y`'s box remains `5`. This concrete demonstration solidifies the logical chain that assignments are snapshots in time, frozen at the exact moment of execution.

Once the mechanics of sequential state-tracking are clear, we present the session's core practice challenge. The instructor displays a scrambled set of four pseudocode lines designed to swap the values of two variables using a temporary third variable, which is a classic AP standard paradigm. Instead of giving the solution, the instructor guides the class through dry-running a broken sequence first—such as writing `a ← b` followed by `b ← a`—to reveal how the original value of `a` gets permanently overwritten and lost. This failure state creates an immediate 'aha' moment, naturally motivating the need for a temporary variable to hold the value of `a` before the overwrite occurs.

To close the session, the instructor facilitates a collaborative rearranging exercise where the students sequence the correct progression: storing `a` in `temp`, copying `b` into `a`, and finally copying `temp` into `b`. We trace this successful execution step-by-step on the whiteboard, updating the variable memory boxes at each line. This leaves students with a robust mental model of sequential dependencies, paving the perfect logical pathway for the branching conditionals and decisions that will be introduced in the next sessions.

tasks: Rearrange scrambled pseudocode statements to execute a correct arithmetic progression.

sessions.title: Boolean Expressions
sessions.description: Construct logic assertions using relational operators and relational conjunctions (AND, OR, NOT).
sessions.sessionOutline:
Begin the session by establishing the ultimate foundation of computer decision-making: the Boolean value. Introduce the concept that everything a computer decides eventually boils down to a simple, binary choice of True or False. Use the whiteboard to write down the basic relational operators: equal to (=), not equal to (≠), greater than (>), less than (<), greater than or equal to (≥), and less than or equal to (≤). Write simple comparison statements on the board, such as '5 > 3' and '4 ≤ 2', and ask the class to call out whether they evaluate to True or False. The key insight to emphasize here is that relational operators take in numbers or strings but always output a single Boolean value, which acts as the raw material for more complex algorithms.

Next, transition to combining these basic comparisons using the logical conjunctions: AND, OR, and NOT. Draw three distinct tables on the whiteboard to represent their behaviors. Focus heavily on a major point of confusion for beginners: the inclusive nature of the logical 'OR'. In daily English, 'you can have soup or salad' usually means you can only have one, but in computer science, 'A OR B' is True if A is true, if B is true, or if both are true. Contrast this with 'AND', which requires both conditions to be simultaneously satisfied, and 'NOT', which acts as an inverter. Use relatable examples on the board, like 'Is it raining AND do I have an umbrella?' to explain how these operators guard actions in real life.

Now, demonstrate the formal order of operations for evaluating compound Boolean expressions. Introduce a multi-layered expression on the whiteboard, such as 'NOT (5 > 3) AND (2 < 4 OR 1 == 1)'. Show the logical derivation step-by-step, mimicking a computer's evaluation path. Explain that expressions inside parentheses are always evaluated first, followed by NOT, then AND, and finally OR. Use different colored markers to underline each sub-expression as it resolves to True or False, visually shrinking the complex formula until it collapses into a final single Boolean. This systematic, visual reduction prevents cognitive overload and teaches students how to 'dry-run' expressions during exams.

Conclude the session with an interactive practice scenario designed to expose common logical fallacies. Write an expression like 'NOT (x > 5 AND y < 10)' with specific values assigned to x and y. Guide the students through resolving the inner parentheses first before applying the outer 'NOT'. Watch out for the common mistake where students try to distribute the 'NOT' operator incorrectly without flipping the internal comparison signs (a preview of De Morgan's Laws). Wrap up by explaining that mastering these Boolean derivations is the direct gatekeeper to understanding conditional execution pathing, which is the exact topic of the next session.

tasks: Evaluate the truth values of expressions combining AND, OR, and NOT comparisons.

sessions.title: Conditional Statements
sessions.description: Direct program pathways using conditional constructs (IF, IF-ELSE) based on evaluated boolean outcomes.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Begin the session by drawing a simple, linear road on the whiteboard, representing the sequencing from Session 3.2.2. Immediately branch this road into a fork to visually introduce the power of conditional decision-making. Explain that while sequencing executes every single instruction, conditional statements introduce selective execution—allowing programs to dynamically choose which code blocks to run and which to completely ignore based on the Boolean outcomes decoded in Session 3.2.3. Emphasize that this is the absolute foundation of adaptive software, turning static code into responsive systems. Use the official AP pseudocode syntax on the board, demonstrating both the simple 'IF (condition)' construct and the binary decision 'IF (condition) / ELSE' construct. Point out that the condition inside the parentheses must always evaluate to a single Boolean value: true or false.

Transition into explaining the execution logic of the 'IF-ELSE' structure. On the whiteboard, draw a flow diagram with a diamond representing the conditional test, leading to two mutually exclusive paths. It is critical to address a common student pitfall here: the misconception that both blocks can run, or that the 'ELSE' block is an independent command. Clarify that the 'ELSE' block only executes if and only if the 'IF' condition evaluates to false. Write a basic AP-style example on the board involving numerical comparison (e.g., checking if a score qualifies for a pass) and physically erase or cross out the path that is not taken during a mock execution to reinforce the concept of mutual exclusivity.

Elevate the logical complexity by introducing nested conditional statements, which is a major focus of the AP exam and a frequent source of student errors. On the whiteboard, write a nested code block where an 'IF' statement is nested entirely within the 'ELSE' portion of another conditional. Use colored markers to draw bounding boxes around each nested level, showing how the inner 'IF' is completely dependent on the outer condition failing first. Explain the logical chain of evaluation step-by-step. Explain the 'dangling else' confusion: students often struggle to match an 'ELSE' with its correct parent 'IF' when indentation is ambiguous. Teach them to use bracket alignment and formal indentation tracking to structurally isolate which block belongs to which condition.

Introduce a hands-on dry-run practice on the whiteboard to consolidate these nesting rules. Present a multi-tiered AP pseudocode snippet that determines an output based on two variables, such as 'age' and 'isStudent'. Walk through multiple test cases with different input values. Ask the students to predict the output. This exercise is specifically designed to expose 'lazy evaluation' errors, where students stop tracking logic prematurely, or 'fall-through' errors, where they mistakenly execute subsequent blocks even after a matching condition has already been triggered. Conclude by demonstrating how cleanly tracing these logical branches on a whiteboard builds the exact visual muscle memory required to tackle complex tracing questions under AP exam time constraints.

tasks: Determine the final output value of nested IF-ELSE control structures.

sessions.title: Iteration
sessions.description: Execute block iterations using count-controlled (REPEAT n TIMES) and condition-controlled (REPEAT UNTIL) loops.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this session by addressing the core concept of iteration: why do computers excel at repetitive tasks, and how do programmers harness this power without writing redundant code? The central idea is that loops allow us to execute a block of instructions multiple times, controlled by a specific condition. For a concept-first audience, we introduce this not through technical jargon, but as a universal mechanism—like a runner doing laps on a track until they have completed their target distance or are too tired to continue. This sets up the logical progression from static, linear sequential code to dynamic, looping algorithms that can process variable amounts of data.

Next, we introduce the first major structural loop variant defined in the AP CSP framework: count-controlled iteration, represented as REPEAT n TIMES. We draw a clear distinction between knowing beforehand how many times a loop will execute versus executing a loop based on a changing state. On the whiteboard, we map out a simple example, such as REPEAT 5 TIMES, and trace the execution path. The critical takeaway here is that the loop control variable is managed automatically behind the scenes; the programmer does not need to manually increment a counter. We warn educators to flag a common student misconception here: thinking that 'n' can change dynamically inside the loop to alter the pre-determined iteration count, which is not how standard AP count-controlled loops behave.

We then transition to condition-controlled iteration using the REPEAT UNTIL loop structure, which is the cornerstone of AP CSP pseudocode looping. Unlike 'while' loops found in languages like Python or Java, REPEAT UNTIL executes its inner block *until* the condition evaluates to true. This means the loop continues to run as long as the condition is false, and terminates the moment it becomes true. To visually represent this on the whiteboard, we draw a flowchart side-by-side with the pseudocode, highlighting the evaluation gate at the start of each iteration. We emphasize to students that because the check happens before the body executes, if the termination condition is true at the very beginning, the loop body will not run even once.

To solidify this logic, we introduce a tracing exercise designed to expose the 'off-by-one' error, which is the most frequent logical bug students encounter. On the board, we write an algorithm where a counter variable 'x' starts at 1, and we loop REPEAT UNTIL x > 4, incrementing 'x' by 1 inside. We walk through a trace table line-by-line, showing that when 'x' becomes 4, the condition '4 > 4' is still false, so the loop runs one more time, making 'x' equal to 5. Now, '5 > 4' is true, and the loop terminates. This demonstrates clearly to students that the final value of 'x' is 5, not 4, and the loop body executed exactly 4 times. Tracing this step-by-step prevents students from guessing and teaches them to rely on systematic state tracking.

tasks: Determine the execution count and final loop variable values of a REPEAT UNTIL logic loop.

sessions.title: Tracing an Algorithm
sessions.description: Learn manual desk-checking techniques to step through logic arrays and find edge-case execution bugs.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this whiteboard session by establishing the critical role of 'desk-checking' or manual tracing in programming. In a concept-first public lecture style, we want to dispel the myth that tracing is a remedial skill or a waste of time. Instead, we frame it as an indispensable analytical tool for proving program correctness and diagnosing logical anomalies before a single line of code is executed. Explain to the students that when programs run on a computer, they execute state transitions at millions of operations per second, making it impossible to see the exact moment a bug occurs. Manual tracing allows us to freeze-frame the execution, step by step, simulating the computer's CPU on a physical whiteboard.

Next, introduce the concept of a 'trace table' as a structured matrix. We draw a clean grid on the whiteboard, defining the column headers. To prevent the common misconception that trace tables only track loop counters, we explicitly design our table to monitor four distinct types of variables simultaneously: a loop control index, a running accumulator, a boolean flag status, and an array index or collection element. Walk students through setting up the initial state—the 'row zero'—where variables are assigned their starting values before entering any control loops. We emphasize that skipping this initialization step is the most common reason students miscalculate the first iteration's outcomes on the AP Exam.

Now, initiate the tracing process using a complex, multi-loop pseudocode segment written on the board. The pseudocode should contain a loop that runs exactly five cycles, with internal conditionals that update our tracking variables unevenly. For each cycle, physically write out the step-by-step evaluation of the conditional expressions. For example, explain how the loop counter incrementing from 2 to 3 changes the truth value of an inner conditional statement, which in turn flips our boolean flag and alters the math applied to the accumulator. By visualizing this state-change line-by-line, students see the cascading effects of logical decisions in real time.

During the middle iterations (cycles 2, 3, and 4), actively highlight common edge-case errors that typically trip up students. Warn them about the 'off-by-one' error, pointing out how a loop conditional written as 'UNTIL i > 5' behaves differently than 'UNTIL i >= 5'. Show them how to catch these boundary-value errors by looking at the exact state of the variables at the start and end of each cycle. We will pause here to have the students update their own matrices on their scrap paper, checking if their accumulator matches the whiteboard at cycle 3. This checkpoint is designed to reveal whether they are incorrectly carrying over values from previous iterations or failing to evaluate the loop conditional at the correct execution step.

Finally, we trace the fifth and final loop cycle to demonstrate how the exit criteria are met and how the control flow successfully breaks out of the loop. This final state of our trace table represents the program's output. We wrap up by showing how this systematic visual record of execution states can be used to debug any algorithmic design, providing students with a structured strategy to tackle tricky tracing questions on the AP CSP Exam with absolute precision and confidence.

tasks: Construct a trace table tracking four variables over five loop cycles.

lectures.title: Abstraction and Complex Programs
lectures.description: Structure your code for reuse and scale. Understand how lists, procedural methods, parameters, and simulations manage programming complexity.

sessions.title: Lists and Data Abstraction
sessions.description: Introduce indexed collections of values, detailing how lists manage data sets without requiring distinct individual variables.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this session by confronting the 'variable explosion' problem. Imagine writing a program to manage a simple grocery list of ten items. Using our current toolkit, we would have to declare ten separate variables like item1, item2, item3, and so on. This approach quickly becomes unmanageable if the store expands to a thousand items, making searching, sorting, or editing almost impossible. The whiteboard should be used to visually contrast this chaotic grid of individual variable boxes with a single, ordered cabinet representing a 'List'. Explain that a list is a container that groups multiple values under a single name, which is the foundational concept of data abstraction. It hides the complexity of managing computer memory for individual items and instead presents a unified collection.

Next, the whiteboard transition must introduce how we access individual slots within this container using 'indexes'. It is critical to address a massive point of confusion early: while many professional programming languages like Python or JavaScript start indexing at 0, the AP Computer Science Principles pseudocode framework uses 1-based indexing. Draw a five-slot list on the board and label the slots clearly from 1 to 5. Show that accessing 'myList[1]' retrieves the very first element, and 'myList[5]' retrieves the last element of this five-item list. Explain that an 'index out of bounds' error occurs when a developer attempts to access an index that does not exist, such as index 0 or index 6 in this scenario. Visually demonstrate this error as looking into a non-existent drawer, which causes the program to crash.

Now, introduce the core dynamic operations that make lists powerful: insertion, retrieval, and removal. Use a physical analogy of a line of people waiting. When we 'retrieve' (access) a value, we merely look at who is standing at a specific position without moving them. When we 'insert' an item at a specific index, it doesn't just overwrite what is there; it pushes all subsequent items down the line to make room, changing their index numbers. Conversely, when we 'remove' an item, the gap is immediately filled as all subsequent items shift up to close the space. Run through a dry-run tracing exercise on the whiteboard, starting with an empty list, inserting 'Apple' at index 1, inserting 'Banana' at index 2, then inserting 'Cherry' at index 2. Ask the class to determine what is now at index 3. This visual shifting demonstrates why keeping track of changing indexes is crucial.

Conclude the whiteboard session with a guided practice task that puts these operations into a logical sequence. Direct the students to write a short sequence of instructions—using AP-style pseudocode notation—that starts with a list containing ['A', 'C']. They must write steps to insert 'B' at index 2 to make it alphabetical, retrieve and display the value at index 3, and then remove the item at index 1. This task is specifically designed to reveal whether students understand index shifting. If they fail to realize that removing the first item shifts 'B' to index 1 and 'C' to index 2, use the whiteboard to physically erase and slide the boxes over, reinforcing the dynamic nature of computer science data structures.

tasks: Write code to insert, retrieve, and remove items from a listed set.

sessions.title: Traversing a List
sessions.description: Explore algorithms that loop through lists to search, filter, or transform items.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin by establishing a clear mental model of list traversal as a systematic, step-by-step examination of every item in a container. Under the concept-first public lecture style, we avoid language-specific syntax quirks and instead focus on the core logical construct: a loop paired with an index pointer that marches through the collection from the first element to the last. This concept is vital because it forms the backbone of any data aggregation, filtering, or search task. To make this concrete, we can visualize a conveyor belt of closed boxes (our list) and a single inspector (our loop) who can only look inside one box at a time. This visualization addresses a common beginner misconception that a program can 'see' the entire list simultaneously. We must emphasize that the computer has a narrow field of vision and must examine elements sequentially.

Next, we transition to the primary application: finding the maximum value in an unsorted list of numbers. To teach this logic, we set up a physical analogy on the board. We draw an empty slot labeled 'currentMax' and a sequence of boxes containing the numbers [14, 27, 8, 31, 19]. We explain the logic of initialization: we must start by assuming the first element is our maximum, rather than initializing 'currentMax' to a default like zero. This is a crucial teaching moment for preventing a classic logical bug—if the list only contained negative numbers, initializing our tracker to zero would yield an incorrect result of zero. We write down 'currentMax = list[1]' on the whiteboard to ground this rule.

Now, we dry-run the loop iteration-by-iteration, showing how the algorithm evaluates each subsequent element against our temporary champion. For each step, we write out the comparison explicitly: Is 27 greater than 14? Yes, so we erase 14 and write 27 in the 'currentMax' slot. Is 8 greater than 27? No, so we do nothing. We continue this trace to show how 'currentMax' updates to 31, and then remains 31 when evaluating 19. By visualizing the variable state updating dynamically next to the list, we help students build a solid mental debugger, preparing them to spot errors in conditional logic and boundary conditions.

To wrap up the session and verify understanding, we introduce a brief practice challenge: tracing an algorithm designed to find the minimum value, but with a twist—we ask what happens if the list contains duplicate values or is completely sorted in descending order. This exercise is designed to reveal whether students understand the conditional execution inside the loop and to solidify their understanding of worst-case execution paths. We conclude by highlighting how this linear traversal scales directly with the size of the dataset, setting the stage for future discussions on algorithmic efficiency.

tasks: Trace an algorithm that finds the maximum value inside a list of unsorted numbers.

sessions.title: Procedures and Procedural Abstraction
sessions.description: Define named code subroutines that perform specific tasks, allowing you to reuse logic without repeating block statements.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this session by introducing a common architectural problem in software design: redundancy. Using a concept-first approach, the instructor will write out two highly repetitive code blocks on the physical or virtual whiteboard, such as calculating the area and perimeter of multiple shapes with distinct variable sets. By observing this bloated code, we show how duplication invites bugs and increases maintenance overhead. This leads to the definition of procedural abstraction: wrapping a block of statements into a single, named entity—a procedure—that can be executed repeatedly from anywhere in the program. The key idea here is simplifying the mental model; developers don't need to know the internal logic of a procedure to use it, just as a driver doesn't need to understand the internal combustion engine to step on the gas pedal.

Next, we transition to a whiteboard demonstration to dissect the mechanics of a procedure. The instructor will draw a clear boundary separating the definition of a procedure from its execution or 'call' phase. A common student misconception is thinking that defining a procedure automatically runs the code; we explicitly address this by showing that a procedure is merely a blueprint stored in memory, waiting to be triggered by its unique identifier. We will trace the program's control flow on the whiteboard, using physical arrows to show how execution jumps from the main program block into the procedure's local scope, runs the internal statements, and then returns precisely to the line immediately following the call. This visualization solidifies the sequence of execution and helps students track exactly where they are in the program flow.

To consolidate this understanding, we pivot to a modularization challenge. The instructor presents a messy, unmodularized script containing duplicated mathematical formulas or text-formatting patterns. Students are tasked with locating these redundant operations, isolating the core logic, and wrapping it into a single, cohesive procedure. This exercise serves as a diagnostic tool: if a student struggles to identify the common pattern, they likely need help separating variables from structures. By identifying these redundancies together, students discover that clean, modular code is not just about writing fewer lines, but about building reliable, testable blocks of logic that serve as the foundation for complex program development.

tasks: Locate redundant operations in an unmodularized script and design a single procedure to replace them.

sessions.title: Parameters and Return Values
sessions.description: Pass dynamic arguments into procedures to compute and return generalized outputs to the main execution line.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Begin the session by challenging the class with a design flaw: a procedure that calculates the average of two hardcoded numbers, such as 10 and 20. Ask the students how they would modify this code if they suddenly needed to calculate the average of 50 and 100, or 1000 and 2000. Under traditional logic, they would either have to duplicate the procedure multiple times or write messy global variables. This is where you introduce the whiteboard conceptual drawing: a 'function machine' with physical input slots at the top and an output conveyor belt at the bottom. Explain that parameters are the input slots—dynamic placeholders that allow a single block of code to work with different data every time it is run.

On the whiteboard, write the formal definitions of 'parameters' versus 'arguments' side-by-side to eliminate a very common source of terminology confusion. Define parameters as the formal variables declared in the procedure's header (the placeholders), and arguments as the actual, concrete values passed into those placeholders during a specific function call. Draw an execution flow diagram: on the left, show the main program calling a procedure with arguments; on the right, show the procedure header. Draw bright, clear arrows tracing how the values of the arguments are copied directly into the parameter variables. Emphasize variable scope here: remind students that these parameter variables are strictly local to the procedure and vanish entirely from memory once the procedure finishes executing.

Transition next to the concept of return values, which is historically one of the most difficult concepts for introductory students to grasp. Many beginners confuse 'returning' a value with 'printing' or 'displaying' it. Use a clear real-world analogy: if you send an assistant to buy a coffee, you do not want them to buy it, drink it themselves, and yell 'I drank a cappuccino!' (which is like printing a value inside a procedure). You want them to buy the coffee and physically bring it back to you so you can drink it (which is like returning a value to the main program). Write a side-by-side pseudocode comparison on the board. On one side, show a procedure that simply displays a calculation. On the other side, show a procedure that returns it. Demonstrate that only the returning procedure allows us to save the output into a variable, pass it to another function, or use it in subsequent math equations.

Now, lead the class through the primary whiteboard practice task: writing a custom calculator procedure that computes and returns the average of two numbers. Write AP-style pseudocode: `PROCEDURE calculateAverage(num1, num2)`. Inside the block, write the steps: `sum <- num1 + num2` followed by `avg <- sum / 2` and finally `RETURN avg`. Point directly to the `RETURN` keyword and explain that it acts as an immediate exit signal for the procedure, carrying the value of `avg` back to the exact line where the procedure was called.

Complete the tracing exercise by writing the calling code on the board: `finalGrade <- calculateAverage(85, 95)`. Use a red marker to physically cross out the call `calculateAverage(85, 95)` and write `90` over it, illustrating how the returned value effectively replaces the procedure call in the main thread of execution. Wrap up the session by highlighting how this cycle of parameter passing and returning outputs creates highly reusable, modular code blocks, saving developers thousands of lines of redundant script and making programs infinitely easier to maintain and scale.

tasks: Write a custom calculator procedure with two numeric parameters that returns their computed average.

sessions.title: Simulations
sessions.description: Use random parameters and simplified mathematical rules to simulate complex real-world systems like traffic flows or coin tosses.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this session by introducing the concept of a simulation as an abstracted, executable representation of a real-world system. Because the learner has indicated a preference for a concept-first, public-lecture style, we will frame this around high-level conceptual models rather than deep-dive syntax. The core idea is that computers allow us to model complex systems—from traffic grids to global weather and disease transmission—by stripping away non-essential real-world details. This process of selective omission is a classic example of abstraction, and it is crucial because simulating every microscopic variable is computationally impossible and practically unnecessary. By simplifying, we trade perfect precision for computational feasibility and analytical clarity.

To anchor this intuition, we sketch a virtual whiteboard diagram representing a classic epidemiological model: the Susceptible-Infectious-Recovered (SIR) model. This provides a clean visual flow of state transitions. The teacher should draw three adjacent boxes containing groups of simple stick figures, with arrows indicating the rate of transition from Susceptible to Infectious, and from Infectious to Recovered. We explain that to model how an infectious disease spreads throughout a population, we must make explicit 'simplifying assumptions'. On the whiteboard, we list these assumptions next to our boxes: we assume a closed population with no births or deaths, we assume all individuals interact uniformly with each other, and we assume once someone recovers, they gain permanent immunity. Explaining *why* we make these assumptions helps students understand that without these limits, the math becomes unmanageable for a basic computer program, yet with them, we can still generate useful predictive trends.

A common pitfall for students is equating a simulation with a perfect, 100% accurate prediction. Many assume that if a simulation does not match real-world outcomes exactly, the code is broken. The teacher should explicitly address this misconception by contrasting a simulation's purpose (to test hypotheses and observe general emergent patterns under varying constraints) with a deterministic calculation. We illustrate this by introducing randomized elements (using pseudo-random number generators) to represent the unpredictable behavior of human movement or transmission probability. Even with simplified rules, changing these probability parameters allows us to observe how 'flattening the curve' works conceptually without needing to track the exact minute-by-minute actions of millions of individuals.

We transition into an interactive practice segment where we ask the classroom to analyze our simulated infectious disease model and identify what crucial real-world factors have been omitted. The teacher prompts: 'If we use this simulation to plan hospital capacities, what critical real-world details are we missing that could make our predictions dangerously inaccurate?' We guide students to identify variables like geographic barriers, varied population densities (cities versus rural areas), diverse age groups with varying susceptibility, and changing human behaviors like social distancing. Through this exercise, students practice the critical AP CSP skill of evaluating simulations, recognizing that while simulations are incredibly powerful tools for exploring hypotheses, their outputs are fundamentally constrained by the validity of their underlying assumptions.

tasks: Identify the simplifying assumptions made in a simulation of infectious disease spread.

sessions.title: Algorithmic Efficiency
sessions.description: Compare algorithm execution speeds, distinguishing between linear (sequential) search and logarithmic (binary) search processes.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin our exploration of algorithmic efficiency by presenting a simple, real-world puzzle to the class on the virtual whiteboard: imagine searching for a specific word in a physical dictionary containing thousands of pages. We ask the class whether they would flip page-by-page from the beginning, or open the book in the middle, check the letter, and discard half the pages in one go. This visual and intuitive concept-first analogy unlocks the logical transition from a linear, brute-force approach to a highly structured logarithmic search. The core idea here is that computer scientists do not merely care if an algorithm is correct; they care about how its performance scales as the volume of input data grows. Understanding this scaling behavior is essential for passing the AP Exam and, more importantly, for understanding the constraints of modern large-scale digital systems.

To formalize this, we draw a horizontal line on the board representing an array of sorted elements. We first trace a sequential search, also known as a linear search. We model its execution by checking every single item from index zero up to the end of the list. We emphasize to the students that a sequential search is highly versatile because it makes absolutely no assumptions about the order of the items; it works on both sorted and unsorted lists. However, we highlight the worst-case scenario: if the target value is at the very end of the list or does not exist at all, we must make as many comparisons as there are elements in the list. This linear relationship between list size (N) and the number of operations (N) is labeled on our whiteboard diagram. We warn students of a common AP misconception: assuming that sequential search always takes N steps. We clarify that while the best-case scenario is 1 step (finding it immediately), algorithmic efficiency is traditionally measured by worst-case performance to guarantee limits.

Next, we introduce the concept of binary search as a logarithmic search, highlighting the strict prerequisite that the list must be sorted beforehand. This prerequisite is a major trap on the AP exam, and we must explicitly warn students that applying binary search to unsorted data yields unpredictable, incorrect results. On the whiteboard, we map out the split-and-conquer logic of binary search. We find the middle element, compare it to our target, and show how we instantly discard the entire half of the list that cannot contain our target. We visualize this by crossing out large blocks of our drawn list. We trace this mathematical halving process step-by-step to demonstrate how binary search achieves a logarithmic runtime of log-base-2 of N, which scales exceptionally well for massive datasets.

To solidify this theoretical contrast, we transition into a concrete derivation exercise using a list of exactly 100 sorted values. On the whiteboard, we write out the math for both strategies to find a value that isn't present in the list. For the sequential search, the calculation is straightforward: it requires exactly 100 comparisons to confirm the item is missing. For the binary search, we write down the mathematical sequence of halving: starting at 100, we divide by 2 to get 50, then 25, then 12.5 (which we round to 12 or 13), then 6, then 3, then 1.5, down to a single element. We show that it takes at most 7 steps to find or rule out any value in a sorted list of 100 items. This stark contrast—7 operations versus 100 operations—vividly demonstrates the power of logarithmic scaling.

We conclude this session by pushing the limits of this calculation to show why this efficiency gap matters in the real world. We ask what happens if our sorted list grows to 1,000,000 items. A sequential search would require up to 1,000,000 steps, whereas a binary search, doubling our progress with each cut, would take only about 20 steps. By tracing these numbers on the board, we build an intuitive mathematical bridge for learners, demonstrating that while both algorithms solve the same search problem, their efficiency profiles make them fundamentally different tools for software developers.

tasks: Calculate search steps required by sequential versus binary search methods for a list of 100 sorted values.

sessions.title: Limits of Algorithms and Computing
sessions.description: Analyze theoretical limitations of computers, discussing heuristic solutions, exponential runtimes, and undecidable problems.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this whiteboard session by drawing a sharp line between problems that are hard to solve and problems that are mathematically impossible to solve. Many students carry the misconception that with enough CPU power, memory, or time, any computational problem can eventually be solved. To dismantle this, we structure the board into three zones: Reasonable Time (polynomial or better), Unreasonable Time (exponential/factorial), and Undecidable (completely unsolvable). We first introduce the concept of 'reasonable' vs. 'unreasonable' runtimes. By writing out growth functions side-by-side—such as linear growth versus exponential growth—we visualize how an algorithm that takes 2^n steps becomes practically useless even for a small input size of 50, requiring more time than the age of the universe to complete. 

This leads directly to the concept of heuristics. When a problem has no known reasonable-time solution, computer scientists do not give up; instead, they employ heuristic approaches. We explain a heuristic as an educational shortcut or a 'rule of thumb' that finds an approximate or good-enough solution when finding the absolute optimal solution is computationally impossible within a human lifetime. We use the classic Traveling Salesperson Problem to illustrate this point. Rather than checking every single possible route (which is an unreasonable factorial complexity), a simple heuristic like 'always travel to the nearest unvisited city next' yields a decent route in a fraction of a second. The teacher should highlight that heuristics trade perfection for speed.

Next, we transition from slow algorithms to the ultimate boundary of computer science: undecidable problems. An undecidable problem is not one that takes too long; it is a problem for which it is mathematically impossible to write a single algorithm that will always provide a correct yes-or-no answer for all possible inputs. To make this abstract barrier tangible, we introduce the famous Halting Problem. We draw a flowchart representing a hypothetical program checker called 'WillItHalt(Program, Input)' which returns True if the program runs and eventually stops, and False if it gets stuck in an infinite loop.

To construct the proof by contradiction, we guide the students through a thought experiment. We tell the whiteboard audience to imagine we write a mischievous wrapper program called 'Opposite(Program)'. This new program calls 'WillItHalt' on itself. If 'WillItHalt' says the program will halt, 'Opposite' intentionally enters an infinite loop. If 'WillItHalt' says it will loop forever, 'Opposite' immediately stops. We trace the logical trap: what happens when we run 'Opposite(Opposite)'? If it halts, it must loop; if it loops, it must halt. This logical paradox proves that a perfect, universal halt-checker cannot exist, making the Halting Problem undecidable.

We conclude with a collaborative classification exercise on the whiteboard. The teacher writes down various scenario cards on the board, such as 'finding the absolute shortest path through 100 delivery destinations', 'analyzing a block of code to guarantee it has no bugs or infinite loops', and 'sorting a massive list of user IDs'. We challenge students to classify each scenario. This active practice ensures students can distinguish between tasks that are merely intractable (requiring heuristics) and those that are fundamentally undecidable, solidifying their understanding of algorithmic limits just in time for the AP exam's conceptual questions.

tasks: Classify a programmatic task as either decidable or undecidable using the Halting Problem as a structural analogy.
