units.title: Computer Systems and Networks
units.description: Understand computer architectures and the internet. Learn how hardware components interact, how data packets route around the globe, and how distributed structures scale computing power.

lectures.title: Computer Systems
lectures.description: Examine the hardware components, system software, and abstraction layers that power computational architectures.

sessions.title: Hardware and Software
sessions.description: Examine the roles of the physical CPU, memory arrays, inputs/outputs, and the programs that command them.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Begin the session by bridging the gap between Unit 3's logical code and the physical realities of computer systems. On the center of the whiteboard, draw a large, empty box representing the computer case, and explain that before we can understand complex networks, we must master how a single machine orchestrates its hardware to bring software to life. Introduce the four core pillars of computer hardware: Input devices, the Central Processing Unit (CPU), Random Access Memory (RAM), and Output devices. Emphasize that software is not some magical, formless entity, but a sequence of physical electrical charges that direct physical switches inside these components.

Draw the CPU and RAM as two separate, highly connected blocks on your whiteboard. Explain the fundamental difference between processing and storage, detailing how the CPU acts as the primary execution engine while RAM serves as the volatile workspace. A vital pedagogical move here is addressing the universal student misconception: confusing RAM with secondary storage (like hard drives or SSDs). Explicitly write 'Volatile (RAM) vs. Non-Volatile (Hard Drive)' on the board. Explain that while a game or program is saved permanently on the slow hard drive, it must be copied into the fast, temporary workspace of RAM before the CPU can read and execute its instructions. Use the analogy of a kitchen: the hard drive is the deep pantry across the room, RAM is the cutting board right in front of the chef, and the CPU is the chef executing the recipe.

Now, transition to the core whiteboard exercise which directly addresses the session's practice task: tracing the physical route of a keyboard click. Draw a keyboard on the left side of the board and a monitor on the right. Ask the students, 'What physically happens when you press the key "A" in a text editor?' Trace an arrow from the keyboard to a motherboard bus controller, explaining that the physical key-press closes a switch, sending a specific binary pattern (an electrical signal) through the wires. Show how this signal is temporarily held in RAM while an interrupt signal alerts the CPU.

Next, draw the logic loop within the CPU. Explain that the CPU retrieves the instructions of the text editor program from RAM, decodes what to do with the incoming 'A' keypress, and computes the update. The CPU then writes the updated text data back to a specific region of RAM called the frame buffer. From there, trace the final arrow from RAM to the video card and out to the monitor, where individual pixels are commanded to illuminate in the shape of the character. This step-by-step whiteboard animation of the data route visualizes the computer as a highly structured highway, preventing the misconception that input devices communicate directly with output devices without passing through memory and processor controls.

Conclude the session by having students verbally trace this data route in reverse or explain what would happen if RAM were suddenly cleared mid-process. This diagnostic check confirms if they understand RAM's volatile nature and its role as the critical intermediary. Explain that in the next session, we will peel back the layers of this physical hardware to look at the invisible digital abstractions that allow us to write code without worrying about individual wires and electrical currents.

tasks: Describe the physical route data takes from an input keyboard click through RAM processing to the screen display.

sessions.title: Layers of Abstraction
sessions.description: Explain how hardware uses abstraction barriers, from raw silicon gates up to system applications.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin by introducing the core concept of abstraction through a real-world analogy: driving a car. A driver does not need to understand physical engine cylinders, spark plug timing, or fuel-injection math to navigate a highway; they rely on high-level interfaces like the steering wheel and gas pedal. In computing, we do the same. We organize complex engineering into distinct stacks, where each layer hides the messy details of the layer beneath it. This structured hiding of details is what allows us to write software without manually modulating electrical voltage on silicone chips. If the system fails, we can isolate the failure to a specific tier because the boundaries are so strictly defined.

Now, we build our visual 'abstraction stack' on the whiteboard from the ground up, starting with the lowest logical layer: physical silicon and electrical currents. We explain that at this level, computers only interpret high and low voltages. To make sense of this physical reality, we overlay the binary representation layer, mapping physical high/low voltages to conceptual 1s and 0s. The teacher should sketch simple transistors and wire them together to show how physical silicon structures form logic gates (AND, OR, NOT) to process these bits. This is a crucial conceptual pivot: the hardware logic gates translate electrical inputs into binary-based mathematical logic, serving as the bridge between physical physical hardware and abstract computational operations.

We then step up the stack into system software and user applications. Above the logic gates sits the instruction set architecture and the operating system. The teacher should draw a solid barrier on the board, explaining that the operating system serves as the grand manager, translating complicated machine operations into clean system calls. Above the operating system, we place high-level programming languages and user applications, which are entirely insulated from the physical motherboard layout. The key misconception to actively head off here is that code directly runs on the computer in its written form. Students often forget that high-level code must be compiled or interpreted down through every single layer of the stack to become physical electrical pulses again.

To solidify this hierarchy, we pivot to an interactive whiteboard sorting task. The teacher writes four jumbled elements on the board: a web browser, binary digits, logic gates, and the operating system. We ask the students to order these from lowest abstraction (closest to the hardware) to highest abstraction (closest to the human user). As we trace the path from logic gates to binary, up to the operating system, and finally to the browser application, we discuss why this hierarchy is crucial for modern software development. Without these protective boundaries, a simple web browser update would require rewiring physical silicon—a realization that emphasizes the brilliance of computing abstraction.

tasks: Order computing layers (binary, logic gates, operating system, applications) from lowest abstraction to highest.

sessions.title: Operating Systems
sessions.description: Study how the operating system acts as an intermediary, managing physical hardware resources for applications.
sessions.sessionOutline:
To introduce the Operating System (OS) in a concept-first public lecture style, we begin by painting a picture of a chaotic computer system where every individual application tries to talk directly to the hardware. Imagine a world where a web browser, a music player, and a text editor all try to send electrical signals to the physical speakers or write directly to the same sector of physical memory at the exact same moment. Without a traffic cop, this results in data corruption, system crashes, and security disasters. This narrative hook establishes the absolute necessity of the Operating System as the ultimate intermediary—a specialized layer of software that abstracts away the physical hardware complexities and fairly allocates resources to competing applications.

Next, the whiteboard layout should clearly divide the computational world into three distinct tiers: the Physical Hardware (CPU, RAM, Storage, I/O devices), the Operating System Kernels, and the User Space Applications (like web browsers, games, or document editors). Draw arrows to demonstrate that applications *cannot* touch the hardware directly; they must make request calls to the OS. Introduce the core responsibilities of the OS: processor management (scheduling which program gets CPU time), memory management (allocating chunks of RAM so applications don't overwrite each other's data), file system management, and device communication via drivers. Emphasize that the OS acts as a protective shield and resource distributor, converting complex hardware protocols into standard interfaces that applications can easily use.

To prevent common student misconceptions, carefully unpack the difference between system software and application software. A classic trap for students is thinking that web browsers, word processors, or video games manage computer memory directly because they run 'fast' or 'lag'. Clarify that these client applications merely *request* memory from the OS; it is the OS that decides where that virtual memory physically maps in the RAM chips. On the whiteboard, draw a clear comparative table. On the left side, list typical OS-specific tasks: allocating RAM, handling peripheral signals, enforcing file permissions, and multitasking CPU cycles. On the right side, list application-specific tasks: rendering web pages, executing game logic, and formatting user text document files. This contrast helps students understand that the OS manages the machine, while applications serve the user.

Conclude the session with an interactive scenario-based check for understanding. Present the students with a list of real-world scenarios, such as 'saving a PDF document to a solid-state drive' versus 'converting a document into a PDF format'. Have them trace which parts of these actions are handled by the PDF reader application and which parts are handed off to the OS. Explain that the application converts the document format in its own software space, but the moment a physical write operation occurs on the hard drive, the OS must step in to locate free physical blocks and manage the storage controller. This diagnostic practice reveals whether students can successfully distinguish between purely logical software operations and physical hardware resource coordination.

tasks: Identify system tasks handled specifically by the operating system versus tasks handled by client application software.

sessions.title: System Reliability
sessions.description: Examine why component degradation and physical errors occur, and how hardware architectures mitigate physical failures.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this session by addressing a fundamental physical reality of computing systems: hardware degrades over time. Students often perceive computers as abstract mathematical engines that operate in perfect digital environments. On our physical whiteboard, the instructor should draw a simple diagram of a physical server or a silicon gate to illustrate that digital abstractions are built on vulnerable physical substrates. This introduction shifts the learner's perspective from purely logical thinking to physical realities. Explain that electromigration, thermal stress, and power fluctuations can cause hardware components to degrade or fail unexpectedly. This sets the stage for understanding why system design must account for eventual physical failure rather than assuming permanent hardware perfection.

From this point of view, we introduce the core architectural concept of the single point of failure (SPOF). On the whiteboard, draw a linear chain of components—such as a single power supply feeding a single hard drive connected to a single processor. The logic chain is clear: if any link in this sequence fails, the entire computing system grinds to a halt. Highlight that identifying these structural vulnerabilities is the first duty of system architects. The instructor can preempt a common learner misconception here: simply buying more expensive or higher-quality components does not solve the underlying design issue, as even the most reliable single component will eventually fail.

This realization leads naturally to our main technical solution: physical and architectural redundancy. Redundancy is the intentional duplication of critical components to ensure system reliability even when individual parts degrade or crash. On the whiteboard, transform the linear chain into a redundant architecture. Draw redundant power supplies operating in parallel and mirror drive arrays (RAIDs). Show how if one power line goes dark, a secondary route immediately takes over the load without disrupting the overall processor. Explain that this concept is not just about keeping a system running, but also about protecting data integrity and ensuring continuous uptime, which is vital for any web, enterprise, or space-exploration computing network.

To consolidate this understanding, transition to an interactive design practice on the whiteboard. Present the students with a hypothetical simple network architecture, such as a single local server hosting a critical database with a single network connection. Ask the learners to analyze this setup to locate the single point of failure and design a fault-tolerant backup system. As students suggest solutions, draw their proposed additions on the board—such as redundant servers, backup storage drives, or dual network service providers. This hands-on mapping exercise reveals if students can apply theoretical redundancy to concrete diagrams, and helps clear up any confusion regarding the cost and complexity trade-offs of building complete fault tolerance into real-world networks.

tasks: Analyze a hardware setup and suggest a backup system design to prevent a single point of failure.

lectures.title: The Internet
lectures.description: Trace internet protocols from physical copper cables to logical IPs, DNS, TCP/UDP frameworks, and web architectures.

sessions.title: Physical Internet Infrastructure
sessions.description: Detail physical transport networks, including copper wires, fiber optics, radio waves, and their band-limit parameters.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this session by addressing a common misconception: that the Internet is an ephemeral, magical cloud existing purely in the air. As a concept-first lecture, we must ground the Internet in its raw, physical reality. Introduce the concept of a bit—the fundamental unit of digital information—and explain that to move information, we must physically send bits from one location to another. On the whiteboard, draw three distinct transmission paths: a copper wire (using electricity), a fiber-optic cable (using light), and air space (using radio waves). Emphasize that every email, video, and message must travel through one of these physical mediums.

Deepen the explanation of fiber optics first. Explain that fiber-optic cables use total internal reflection to bounce pulses of light down extremely thin strands of glass. Highlight why this is the backbone of global networks: light travels incredibly fast, suffers minimal signal degradation (attenuation) over vast distances, and can carry massive amounts of data. This allows us to define 'bandwidth'—not as the speed of individual data particles, but as the maximum capacity of a communication channel to transmit data, measured in bits per second. Contrast this with 'latency', which is the time it takes for a single bit to travel from sender to receiver. Explain that while light in glass has low latency and extremely high bandwidth, burying physical cables across oceans is expensive and structurally rigid.

Next, transition to copper cabling and radio waves to illustrate trade-offs. Draw a diagram of a copper cable, explaining that it transmits data via electromagnetic pulses. Copper is highly cost-effective and flexible, but it is highly susceptible to electromagnetic interference (environmental noise) and suffers from significant signal loss over long distances. Then, draw a wireless router emitting radio waves. Explain that wireless transmission uses electromagnetic waves to carry signals through the air. This offers unprecedented mobility but suffers from high latency, limited bandwidth compared to glass fiber, and extreme vulnerability to physical obstacles like concrete walls and weather conditions.

To consolidate this understanding, engage the class in a comparative analysis practice. Have students evaluate a scenario where they must design the network backbone for a new remote research station in a stormy mountain region versus an undersea connection between two continents. Prompt them to compare fiber-optic networks to radio waves in terms of bandwidth capacity, physical speed limit (latency), and susceptibility to physical obstacles or atmospheric noise. Guide them to realize that while radio waves offer easy deployment, their susceptibility to interference makes fiber the only viable choice for critical high-capacity links, solidifying their intuition about the physical compromises inherent in internet design.

tasks: Compare fiber-optic networks to radio waves in terms of physical bandwidth, latency, and susceptibility to environmental noise.

sessions.title: Packets and Packet Switching
sessions.description: Analyze why data is split into standardized packets, routed along separate physical pathways, and reordered at the receiver.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin today's session by addressing a fundamental problem of digital communication: why we cannot simply send massive, unbroken streams of data across the network all at once. If we tried to transmit a single giant file—like a high-definition video—in one continuous block, it would monopolize the physical cables along the path, preventing any other user from communicating until the transfer finished. Worse, if a single bit of that giant file became corrupted or lost during transmission, the entire file would have to be retransmitted from the very beginning. To make students intuitively feel this bottleneck, ask them to imagine a highway where a single gargantuan truck is allowed to block all lanes for hours, versus breaking that truck's cargo down into hundreds of small, agile cars that can weave through different streets. This visualization unlocks the core concept of packet switching: breaking large digital payloads into small, manageable, standardized units called packets.

Next, we build a clear, visual model of a packet on our whiteboard. Draw a simple rectangle representing a single packet and divide it into two key sections: the Header and the Payload. Explain that the Payload contains the actual fragment of the user's data (such as a tiny piece of an image or a syllable of an audio file), while the Header contains critical metadata needed for delivery. This metadata includes the sender's IP address, the receiver's IP address, the packet's total size, and a sequence number (e.g., 'Packet 3 of 4'). Emphasize to students that sequence numbers are the magic key to packet switching. Because packets are routed independently, they may arrive out of order, or some may take longer scenic routes. The sequence number ensures that the receiving computer has the logical blueprint to reassemble the randomized fragments into the original, coherent file.

Now, we transition to tracing how these packets travel across a decentralized network. Sketch a simplified web of interconnected nodes (representing routers) on the whiteboard. Label four nodes as Router A, B, C, and D, with a starting sender and a destination receiver. We introduce a four-packet message and trace each packet's journey individually. As we draw their paths, deliberately route Packet 1 through A and B, Packet 2 through C and D, Packet 3 through B and D, and Packet 4 along whatever route remains. Explain that this dynamic routing happens in real-time based on network congestion, bandwidth availability, and physical link failures. This highlights a crucial AP CSP concept: there is no centralized authority directing traffic. Each router simply makes local, optimal decisions on where to pass a packet next.

At this stage, we address a major student misconception: the belief that packets must arrive in the exact order they were sent. Students often assume that because Packet 1 left first, it must arrive first. Show how a physical bottleneck at Router B might delay Packet 1, causing Packet 2 and Packet 3 to arrive at the destination first. On the whiteboard, show the receiver's buffer holding '[Empty], Packet 2, Packet 3, Packet 4'. Walk through how the receiving computer patiently waits, receives Packet 1 last, and then uses the sequence numbers in the headers to reorder the data stream perfectly before presenting it to the application layer. This step-by-step trace demonstrates how the physical chaos of the internet is resolved through structured logical protocols.

To consolidate this understanding, introduce the interactive tracing exercise. On the board, draw a network graph with six nodes and assign varying transit delays to each connection. Give the students a four-packet message ('H', 'E', 'L', 'P') with corresponding sequence numbers 1, 2, 3, and 4. Challenge them to calculate the arrival order of the packets at the destination node when certain routes become heavily congested or drop offline entirely. This practice task is designed to reveal if students understand that packets travel independently and can arrive out of order, while reinforcing their ability to logically reconstruct the original message using header metadata. Wrap up by reinforcing that packet switching is what makes the internet resilient, scalable, and fair for millions of simultaneous users.

tasks: Trace a data stream broken into four packets as they travel across a simulated switching web, and put them back in order.

sessions.title: Internet Protocol Addresses
sessions.description: Explain hierarchical addressing schemes, comparing IPv4's limited address pool with the expanded capacities of IPv6.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this whiteboard session by establishing the core metaphor of the Internet Protocol (IP) address as a physical mailing address. Just as a postal system requires a unique, structured identifier to route a letter to a specific house, every device connected to the Internet needs a unique numerical identifier to receive data packets. The crucial point for students to grasp early on is that these addresses are not random strings of numbers; they are highly structured, hierarchical entities. This hierarchy is what allows global routers to send packets toward a general destination (like a country or network) before having to resolve the specific individual device, preventing the global routing tables from collapsing under their own weight.

To build this intuition on the whiteboard, we draw a parallel between a mailing address (Country -> State -> City -> Street -> House Number) and an IP address. We explain that the left-most bits of an IP address identify the network, while the right-most bits identify the specific host on that network. This design choice is fundamental because routers along the path do not need to know where every single computer on Earth is; they only need to know how to reach the network portion. We will write a sample IP address on the board and visually split it down the middle, labeling the left side as 'Network ID' and the right side as 'Host ID' to anchor this logic.

Next, we introduce the historical standard: IPv4 (Internet Protocol version 4). On the whiteboard, we write a typical IPv4 address such as '192.168.1.25'. We dissect this notation by showing that it consists of four numbers separated by dots, known as dot-decimal notation. We explicitly demonstrate that each of these four segments represents exactly one byte (8 bits) of data, which can range from 0 to 255. By calculating 4 segments multiplied by 8 bits, we prove that IPv4 addresses are 32-bit values. We then run the math on the board: 2 raised to the 32nd power, yielding approximately 4.29 billion unique addresses. 

At this point, we introduce the historical tension: with billions of smartphones, smart appliances, and global servers online, we have completely run out of unique IPv4 addresses. This problem introduces a natural transition to IPv6 (Internet Protocol version 6). We write a sample IPv6 address on the board, such as '2001:0db8:85a3:0000:0000:8a2e:0370:7334'. We guide students through its structure: it uses hexadecimal notation (0-9 and a-f) instead of decimal, split into eight groups of four hexadecimal digits separated by colons. We point out that each hexadecimal digit represents 4 bits, meaning each group represents 16 bits, totaling a massive 128-bit address space. We write 2 to the 128th power on the board, explaining that this yields over 340 undecillion addresses—essentially a virtually infinite pool that can easily accommodate every grain of sand on Earth having its own IP address.

To prevent common student misconceptions, the teacher should actively address two areas of confusion. First, students often misidentify hexadecimal characters in IPv6, mistakenly thinking letters outside the 'a' through 'f' range (like 'g' or 'z') are valid. Second, students frequently confuse the dot-decimal 8-bit limit of IPv4 (max 255 per segment) with the hexadecimal 16-bit limit of IPv6 groups (max ffff per segment). We will write a mixed set of invalid formats on the board, such as '256.100.0.1' (invalid IPv4 due to 256) and '2001:0db8::g123' (invalid IPv6 due to 'g'), explicitly inviting students to spot the syntax violations. This diagnostic checkpoint ensures they can reliably distinguish standard formats before moving to the next system layer.

tasks: Identify whether a set of address formats conform to the logical syntax standards of IPv4 or IPv6.

sessions.title: Routing
sessions.description: Trace how dynamic routers send packets along the most efficient pathways, avoiding congested links without a centralized controller.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this session by addressing a fundamental question: How do millions of data packets navigate the vast, tangled web of the global internet to reach their destinations without a central coordinator or 'master computer' directing traffic? On the whiteboard, draw a scattered network of five or six nodes labeled with letters (A through F), connected by lines representing communication links. Explain that this represents a tiny slice of the internet. The goal of this session is to build a deep, concept-first understanding of dynamic routing, illustrating how packets make independent, real-time decisions at each hop based on local conditions rather than a global master plan.

Introduce the concept of a 'router' as a specialized computer whose sole job is to forward data along this network. Rather than knowing the entire path from source to final destination, each router only needs to decide who to pass the packet to next. Use the analogy of a mail delivery system where a letter traveling from New York to Tokyo isn't directed by a single mailman walking the whole distance; instead, local post offices forward the mail to the next major transit hub along the way. Explain that this decentralized architecture is what makes the internet incredibly resilient, scalable, and cost-effective. Each router maintains a local routing table—essentially a cheat sheet indicating the best next step based on the packet's final address.

Now, introduce the dynamic nature of routing. On the whiteboard network, assign arbitrary weights or 'costs' to the links between nodes to represent factors like latency, physical distance, or congestion (e.g., link A-B has a cost of 1, while A-C has a cost of 5 due to traffic). Walk through a scenario where a packet travels from Node A to Node D. At first, the packet takes the path with the lowest cumulative cost. But what happens if a link suddenly breaks or becomes severely congested? On the board, physically cross out one of the active links (e.g., link B-C). Show how the routers dynamically detect this failure and re-route subsequent packets along an alternative path (like A-C-D), even if it has a higher initial cost. This demonstrates the property of fault tolerance—the ability of a system to continue functioning properly in the event of the failure of some of its components.

Address a common misconception here: students often assume that there must be a central traffic controller managing these updates, or that routers need to know the status of every single connection globally. Clarify that this is false. Routers communicate only with their immediate neighbors, sharing small routing table updates dynamically. This localized, peer-to-peer sharing propagates outward, allowing the entire network to self-heal and adapt organically without any centralized bottleneck. Explain that if the internet relied on a central coordinator, that coordinator would be a single point of failure; if it went down, the entire global network would collapse.

Conclude the session with a hands-on whiteboard exercise designed to test this logic chain. Present a map of seven nodes with various link costs. Instruct the class to trace a packet's route from start to finish, calculating the path with the lowest overall cost. Then, simulate a real-world network failure by declaring that a critical, high-speed backbone link has gone offline. Have the class recalculate the new fastest path. This exercise reveals whether students truly grasp how routers adapt dynamically to real-time topology changes and helps solidify the core AP CSP concept of redundant, fault-tolerant network design.

tasks: Compute the fastest path for a data packet across a routing map when key communication lines drop offline.

sessions.title: The Domain Name System
sessions.description: Study the distributed DNS hierarchy, which maps human-friendly website domains to machine-readable IP addresses.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this session by addressing a simple but profound human-centric design problem on the internet: humans are terrible at remembering long strings of numbers, while routers can only process packets using structured IP addresses. If you want to visit a website, typing an IP address like 192.0.2.1 is counterintuitive and error-prone. To resolve this, the internet relies on the Domain Name System, or DNS, which functions as the global address book of the internet. It is essential to emphasize that DNS is not a single, giant, centralized database; if it were, that single server would immediately crash under the weight of billions of daily global queries, creating a catastrophic single point of failure. Instead, the DNS is a highly distributed, hierarchical database designed to share the load and ensure high availability.

To help students visualize this hierarchy, draw an inverted tree structure on the whiteboard. At the absolute top is the root zone, represented by a single dot (.). Just below the root are the Top-Level Domain (TLD) servers, which handle suffixes like .com, .org, and .edu. Below those are the Authoritative Name Servers, which belong to specific organizations or hosting providers and hold the actual IP addresses for specific domain names (such as example.com). Introduce the local DNS recursive resolver, often provided by an ISP or a public service like Google (8.8.8.8), which acts as a personal helper or 'detective' for the user's browser, running around the world to find the correct IP address so the user doesn't have to.

Walk students through the step-by-step resolution process using a storytelling approach. A user types 'wikipedia.org' into their browser. The browser first checks its local cache. If it is not found, it queries the local recursive resolver. The resolver, lacking the answer, first asks the Root Name Server. The Root server doesn't know the exact IP, but it recognizes the '.org' suffix and points the resolver to the '.org' TLD server. The resolver then queries the '.org' TLD server, which directs it to the authoritative name server for wikipedia.org. Finally, the resolver queries the authoritative server, retrieves the IP address, delivers it back to the computer, and the computer caches it for future use so it doesn't have to repeat this trip. Emphasize that the user's computer only asks once (a recursive query), while the recursive resolver does the heavy lifting of jumping from server to server (iterative queries).

A common student misconception is that DNS changes must happen instantly across the entire internet. Address this by explaining Time-to-Live (TTL) values. When a website owner updates their server's IP address, older records remain cached in resolvers worldwide until their TTL expiration timers run out, which explains why website migrations can take hours to propagate. Another common point of confusion is assuming that the DNS itself hosts the website's files; clarify that DNS only provides the directions (the IP address), and it is the subsequent HTTP request that actually retrieves the website's content.

Conclude with an interactive whiteboarding practice task where students must map out and order the resolution steps. Give them a scenario where a user queries a sub-domain, such as 'news.bbc.co.uk'. Have them draw the paths and label the order of operations from the recursive resolver to the root server, to the '.uk' TLD, to the '.co.uk' server, and finally to the authoritative server. This exercise is designed to reveal whether students understand the hierarchy of domain names (reading right-to-left) and how the iterative resolution query flows from the top of the tree down to the specific leaf node.

tasks: Order the resolution steps taken by a browser query from a root name server down to the authoritative domain server.

sessions.title: TCP and UDP
sessions.description: Examine transport protocols, comparing reliable, verified connections (TCP) with fast, unverified transmissions (UDP).
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin by introducing the Transport Layer of the Internet, explaining to students that while IP addresses handle the routing of packets from machine to machine, we need a higher-level protocol to manage how those packets are delivered and assembled for specific applications. Using a classic postal service analogy, we explain that if IP is the delivery truck that gets a box of mixed-up puzzle pieces to your physical front door, the Transport Layer protocols are the internal rules we use to reconstruct the puzzle and ensure no piece was dropped in transit. Since the learner feedback suggests a concept-first, public-lecture style, we will focus heavily on conceptual clarity and intuitive, real-world analogies before diving into technical details.

Next, we introduce the Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) by walking through its primary design goal: absolute reliability. Teachers should draw a 'three-way handshake' on the whiteboard (SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK) to show how TCP establishes a reliable connection before any actual data is sent. Explain how TCP numbers each packet and requires the receiver to send back an acknowledgment (ACK). If a packet is lost, the sender detects the missing ACK and retransmits that specific packet. Address a common student misconception here: students often think 'reliable' means packets never get lost; we must clarify that packets get lost all the time on the physical internet, but TCP is reliable because it has built-in mechanisms to detect that loss and recover from it. Explain that this guarantees that files like emails, website code (HTML/CSS), and software downloads arrive exactly as intended, without a single corrupt bit.

We then contrast this heavy-duty reliability with the User Datagram Protocol (UDP). On the whiteboard, draw UDP as a simple fire-and-forget mechanism. There is no handshake, no packet numbering, no acknowledgments, and no retransmission. If a packet is lost, it is gone forever, and the stream simply moves on. This lack of overhead makes UDP incredibly fast and lightweight. Address the common misconception that 'unreliable' means UDP is a poorly designed or 'bad' protocol; explain that UDP is deliberately designed this way because some applications prioritize speed and real-time delivery over perfect accuracy. If you are in a live video call or playing a fast-paced online game, a delayed packet (like an audio frame from three seconds ago) is completely useless; you would rather just drop it and receive the current live frame immediately.

To solidify these concepts, we transition into an interactive practice session where we analyze specific digital activities. The teacher will present three scenarios on the board: streaming music, sending an email, and playing a real-time multiplayer online game. We ask the students to evaluate the tradeoffs of each. For email, we show that a dropped packet means a corrupted message, so TCP is mandatory. For online gaming, a minor glitch is acceptable but latency (lag) caused by waiting for retransmitted packets would ruin the game, making UDP the ideal choice. For audio streaming, we can discuss how modern platforms might use TCP with a large buffer, or UDP for ultra-low latency live broadcasts, showing that engineering is all about matching the right protocol to the right user experience.

tasks: Select the most appropriate protocol (TCP or UDP) for audio streaming, email transmission, and online gaming.

sessions.title: HTTP and the World Wide Web
sessions.description: Understand how HTTP operates at the application layer to request and transfer HTML assets over the web.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this session by establishing a clear distinction between the physical and transport mechanisms of the Internet we have previously discussed (like routing, packets, and TCP) and the application layer that sits on top: the World Wide Web. Students frequently confuse the Internet with the Web. Introduce the concept of the Internet as the physical network of connected computers, while the Web is an application layer system of interlinked hypertext documents accessed via the Internet. Use the whiteboard to sketch a quick layered stack, placing HTTP at the very top (Application) and tracing how it relies on the TCP transport layer below it to carry out its requests seamlessly. This sets up the concept-first explanation of HTTP as the standardized language that web browsers and servers use to communicate with each other.

Next, walk the students through the mechanics of an HTTP GET request. Draw a simple client (represented by a computer browser) on the left side of the whiteboard and a web server on the right. Explain that when a user types a URL or clicks a link, the browser generates an plain-text request. Write a simplified raw HTTP GET request header on the board to demystify it—showing lines like 'GET /index.html HTTP/1.1' and 'Host: www.example.com'. Emphasize that HTTP is entirely text-based and stateless, meaning each request is handled as a brand-new, isolated transaction. Warn teachers about a common student misconception here: many believe the server maintains an active, conscious 'connection' with them throughout their entire browsing session. Clarify that HTTP requests are transactional; a request is sent, a response is returned, and the transaction is closed.

Transition to the server's response. On the whiteboard, draw an arrow back from the server to the client. Write out the structure of a standard HTTP response, beginning with the status line. This is the perfect moment to demystify common HTTP status codes that students encounter daily, such as 200 OK (success), 404 Not Found (resource missing), or 500 Internal Server Error (server-side crash). Beneath the headers, write the payload, which is typically the HTML, CSS, or image assets requested. Highlight that a single web page often requires dozens of individual HTTP GET requests—one for the initial HTML structure, and then subsequent requests for every image, stylesheet, and script referenced inside that HTML document.

Finally, lead the class into an interactive whiteboard sketching exercise. Instruct the students to draw their own step-by-step sequence diagram representing a user loading a simple webpage containing one text file and one image asset. Their diagrams should map out the initial TCP handshake implicitly, followed by the explicit HTTP GET request for the HTML file, the server's 200 OK response with the HTML content, the browser parsing the HTML to discover the image link, and the subsequent HTTP GET request and response for that image. While students sketch, walk around to catch errors—particularly students forgetting that the image requires its own separate request-response loop, or forgetting to include HTTP status codes. Conclude the session by summarizing how this application-layer handshake sits at the pinnacle of the entire network architecture, translating complex packet-switched routing into the rich, visual Web experience we use every day.

tasks: Sketch a step-by-step model showing an HTTP GET request and the server's subsequent HTTP response.

lectures.title: Parallel and Distributed Computing
lectures.description: Understand how software scales. Compare sequential, parallel, and distributed computing models while calculating processing speedups.

sessions.title: Sequential Computing
sessions.description: Analyze sequential computing, where operations execute one by one in order.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Begin the session by introducing a simple, physical analogy to anchor the concept of sequential computing. Ask the class to imagine a single chef preparing a three-course meal alone in a small kitchen. The chef must bake the bread, roast the vegetables, and simmer the soup. Because there is only one chef and one oven, these tasks must occur strictly one after another. This logical flow mirrors sequential computing, where a single central processing unit (CPU) executes computer instructions in a precise, consecutive order, one instruction at a time.

On the physical or virtual whiteboard, draw a horizontal timeline to visualize this execution model. Sketch three blocks labeled Task A (3 seconds), Task B (5 seconds), and Task C (2 seconds) placed end-to-end. Use this visual to demonstrate that Task B cannot begin until Task A is completely finished at the 3-second mark, and Task C must wait until Task B finishes at the 8-second mark. Write out the fundamental formula on the board: Total Time = Time(A) + Time(B) + Time(C). Emphasize that in sequential computing, the total execution time is always the direct sum of the individual task times, scaling linearly as more tasks are added.

Address a very common student misconception here: that sequential computing is an 'obsolete' or 'bad' approach because modern computers have multiple cores. Explain that sequential execution is actually the bedrock of computer science because it guarantees deterministic logic and predictability. Introduce the concept of data dependency to explain why we cannot always run things at the same time. For instance, point out that you cannot calculate a sales tax (Task B) until you have retrieved the price of the item (Task A). In this case, Task B has a hard dependency on Task A, meaning a sequential flow is logically required to prevent system errors or garbage data.

Conclude the session with a brief, interactive processing-time measurement exercise. Write a scenario on the board involving a web server that must perform three sequential operations: authenticating a user (40 milliseconds), querying a database (120 milliseconds), and rendering a webpage (60 milliseconds). Have the students calculate the total processing time (220 milliseconds) and explain why these steps must run sequentially rather than simultaneously. This exercises their computational tracing skills and solidifies their understanding of basic execution overhead before they transition to parallel setups.

tasks: Measure the total processing time of a sequential sequence of tasks.

sessions.title: Parallel Computing
sessions.description: Examine parallel computing setups where programs are split into subtasks that run at the same time on a single computer.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this session on the whiteboard by drawing a sharp contrast to our previous discussion of sequential execution. Start by sketching a single, overworked CPU core handling a long queue of instructions one by one. Contrast this immediately with a multi-core processor diagram on the same board, showing four distinct CPU cores sharing a single pool of system memory. Explain that parallel computing is specifically defined as a model where a program is broken down into smaller, independent subtasks that run simultaneously on multiple processors or cores within a single computer system. This distinction is critical: students often conflate parallel computing with distributed computing across the internet, so emphasize that here, we are working within the boundaries of a single physical machine with shared memory.

To build a strong physical intuition, write a concrete processing problem on the board. Suppose a program needs to apply a color filter to a digital image containing 1,000 pixels, and processing each pixel takes exactly 1 millisecond. Sequentially, a single processor must loop through all 1,000 pixels in order, taking 1,000 milliseconds. Now, draw a diagram showing how this image can be sliced into four quadrants of 250 pixels each. Assign each quadrant to one of four independent processor cores. Ask the class to determine the theoretical execution time. It becomes clear that because the processors work concurrently, the entire image is processed in just 250 milliseconds. This visual comparison anchors the definition of parallel processing in a real-world, intuitive scenario.

Next, address a major conceptual pitfall that many introductory students fall into: the assumption of perfect efficiency. Students often believe that if you throw ten times the number of processors at any given problem, it will always run ten times faster. On the whiteboard, introduce the reality of 'overhead' and 'sequential dependencies.' Explain that before the processors can start, a master thread must split the image data and distribute it, and afterwards, it must combine the results back together. Draw these coordination phases as sequential blocks at the beginning and end of the parallel execution timeline. This demonstrates that even in a highly parallel setup, the overall time is bound by these non-parallelizable stages.

Conclude the session with an interactive practice scenario on the board. Present a hypothetical task: a database search that takes 60 seconds sequentially. Assume that 10 seconds of this task must remain strictly sequential (such as initializing the search parameters and saving the final report), while the remaining 50 seconds can be perfectly split among 5 processors. Have students visually map out the timeline on their own note-taking boards to compute the new total processing time. This exercise reveals whether students grasp how to separate a task into its parallelizable and sequential components, setting a solid foundation for the formal speedup calculations they will perform later.

tasks: Compare processing times when running a task sequentially versus splitting it across multiple processors.

sessions.title: Distributed Computing
sessions.description: Examine distributed networks where multiple individual computers work together over a network to solve complex problems.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Begin the session by bridging the gap from parallel computing to distributed computing. On the left side of the whiteboard, sketch a quick diagram of a single computer with multiple cores sharing a single pool of memory. Contrast this by drawing the distributed computing model on the right side: multiple independent computer systems, each with its own processor, memory, and storage, linked together only by network connections. Explain to the class that while parallel computing relies on internal high-speed buses within one physical machine, distributed computing leverages separate, autonomous machines communicating over a local network or the Internet. This shift is crucial because it allows us to scale far beyond the hardware limits of any single physical supercomputer, tapping into vast, collective computing power.

Use the whiteboard to walk through the fundamental mechanics of how these independent systems coordinate. Since they do not share physical memory, they must pass messages to share data and coordinate tasks. Draw arrows representing data packets traveling across the network between the nodes. Highlight the central trade-off: distributed computing offers massive scalability, but it introduces network latency and potential communication bottlenecks. Address a common student misconception here: many beginners confuse 'parallel' with 'distributed' because both execute tasks simultaneously. Emphasize that the key differentiator is memory and physical location—parallel systems share memory locally, whereas distributed systems operate across separate physical boundaries and rely entirely on network communication.

Transition into the core challenge of handling massive datasets, directly addressing the practice task of analyzing data too large to fit on a single server. Present a hypothetical scenario: a data analysis firm needs to process a 100-Terabyte dataset, but the largest server available only has 16 Terabytes of storage. On the whiteboard, illustrate the concept of data partitioning. Show how the massive dataset is sliced into smaller, manageable chunks and distributed across a cluster of ten or twenty individual computers. Each computer processes its local chunk of data independently and simultaneously, and then transmits only the summary results back to a coordinator node. This demonstrates how distributed computing turns an impossible, memory-restricted bottleneck into a highly scalable, concurrent task.

Wrap up the session with an interactive scenario-based practice moment. Ask students to design a distributed approach for a search engine counting keyword occurrences across billions of web pages. Prompt them to explain how they would divide the web pages among a fleet of servers and how they would aggregate the final counts. Use their responses to highlight that distributed systems are not just faster, they are the only viable solution when datasets exceed physical hardware boundaries. Conclude by reinforcing that understanding these distributed patterns is essential for appreciating how modern global cloud infrastructure, from search engines to social media networks, functions at scale.

tasks: Explain how distributed networks analyze datasets too large to fit on a single server.

sessions.title: Redundancy and Fault Tolerance
sessions.description: Explain how duplicate components keep networks running even when individual parts fail.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Begin the session by framing a fundamental truth of computer systems: hardware will eventually fail. On the physical whiteboard, draw a simple line connecting Node A to Node B, and then to Node C. Ask students what happens if the router at Node B loses power or if a backhoe cuts the fiber optic line. The answer is immediate system-wide failure; communication between A and C is severed. Use this stark reality to introduce the concept of fault tolerance—the capability of a network to continue operating even when individual components fail. Explain that the secret to achieving fault tolerance is physical redundancy, which is the intentional inclusion of duplicate components or alternative communication pathways that are not strictly necessary for basic operations but are vital for resilience.

Now, pivot to sketching a more robust, web-like network diagram on the board. Create nodes labeled A, B, C, D, and E. Connect A to both B and C; connect B to D and E; connect C to D and E; and finally, connect D to E. Underneath this diagram, define 'redundant paths' as multiple distinct routes that data packets can take to travel from a source to a destination. Walk the students through a logical tracking exercise: if Node A wants to send a message to Node E, identify all the available paths (A-B-E, A-B-D-E, A-C-E, A-C-D-E). This visual helps students realize that having multiple routes means the network does not rely on a single golden path.

To deepen their conceptual understanding, introduce a critical trap that many students fall into: confusing 'redundancy' with 'inefficiency' or 'waste.' Address this misconception head-on. Explain that while building redundant lines costs more money and resources initially, it is the only way to prevent catastrophic failures. Use the whiteboard to illustrate a 'single point of failure' bottleneck. Draw a complex, highly redundant cluster of nodes on the left side of the board and another on the right side, but connect the two clusters using only a single bridge router, Node X. Show how, despite the massive internal redundancy of both sides, a single crash of Node X completely disconnects the two halves of the network. This visual demonstrates that redundancy must be distributed strategically to achieve true fault tolerance.

Transition into an active whiteboard challenge. Present the students with a specific scenario using the 5-node network drawn earlier: 'If Router B suddenly crashes and goes completely offline, can Node A still successfully transmit data to Node E?' Guide the students to physically trace the surviving pathways on the board. They should observe that while paths utilizing B (A-B-E and A-B-D-E) are severed, the traffic can seamlessly reroute through the southern path via Router C (A-C-E or A-C-D-E). Emphasize that the internet's IP routing protocols do this dynamic recalculation automatically, allowing the network to heal itself in real-time.

Conclude the session by summarizing how this decentralized, redundant design scale-proofs the modern internet. Explain that AP questions frequently ask students to look at network topology graphs and identify whether a system is fault-tolerant or to determine the minimum number of line cuts required to isolate a specific node. Give them a quick rule of thumb to write down: if every node has at least two independent connections to the rest of the network, the system can survive any single point failure. This structural resilience is what keeps global communications alive every second of the day.

tasks: Identify paths in a network diagram that are redundant, and determine if the network can survive a single router crash.

sessions.title: Benefits and Limits of Parallelization
sessions.description: Calculate processing speedups and analyze why sequential dependencies limit parallel efficiency.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Begin the session by confronting a common student misconception: the assumption that doubling the number of processors will automatically cut the execution time of a program in half. On the whiteboard, draw a simple timeline of a program that has tasks that must happen one after another, such as reading a file before processing it, followed by tasks that can run simultaneously, like performing calculations on different parts of an array. Explain that no matter how many processors we throw at a problem, the portion of the program that is strictly sequential acts as a hard limit on how fast the program can run. This sets up the conceptual necessity of measuring 'speedup' to evaluate efficiency.

Next, mathematically define and derive the Speedup formula on the whiteboard. Write out Speedup = (Sequential Execution Time) / (Parallel Execution Time). To make this concrete, break down the parallel execution time into two components: the portion of the task that must run sequentially and the portion that can be parallelized, divided by the number of processors. Use simple variables to represent these parts, showing how as the number of processors increases, the parallel portion's time shrinks toward zero, leaving only the sequential portion as the absolute floor of execution time. Emphasize that this mathematical reality is known as Amdahl's Law, which serves as the theoretical boundary of parallelization.

Illustrate the concept of sequential dependencies using a visual dependency graph on the board. Draw nodes representing tasks and arrows representing dependencies. If Task C requires the outputs of both Task A and Task B, Task C cannot begin until both are complete, meaning Task C has a sequential dependency. Explain that this sequence creates a 'critical path'—the longest sequence of dependent tasks. Students often struggle to identify which parts of a problem can actually run in parallel; highlighting these directional arrows helps them visually isolate parallel blocks from sequential bottlenecks.

Address the limit of infinite processors to dismantle the 'infinite speedup' myth. Ask the students what happens to the overall runtime if we have one million processors. Guide them to see that even with an infinite number of processors, the sequential portion of the code still takes the exact same amount of time. Use a concrete scenario on the board: if a program takes 100 seconds to run sequentially, and 10% of that program must remain sequential, the absolute fastest the program can ever run is 10 seconds, yielding a maximum theoretical speedup of 10x, regardless of how many processors are added.

Conclude with a guided whiteboard practice calculation modeled after AP-style questions. Write down a scenario where a data analysis program takes 80 seconds on a single processor, where 60 seconds of the program can be run in parallel and 20 seconds must run sequentially. Have the students calculate the overall execution time and speedup when running on 2 processors, 4 processors, and an infinite number of processors. Walk through the arithmetic step-by-step, showing how to isolate the parallel chunk, divide it by the processor count, add the sequential overhead back in, and then divide the original sequential time by this new parallel time to find the final speedup factor. This systematic calculation solidifies their understanding of workload efficiency.

tasks: Use parallel calculation speedup formulas to solve workload efficiency problems.
