units.title: Impact of Computing
units.description: Examine the social, legal, and ethical dimensions of computing. Analyze issues surrounding computing bias, access divides, digital privacy, and cryptography, while exploring the responsibilities of software developers.

lectures.title: Computing Innovations and Society
lectures.description: Explore the balance between the benefits and the unintended social risks of rapid technological development.

sessions.title: Benefits of Computing Innovations
sessions.description: Analyze how computing advancements improve communication, collaboration, and medicine across the globe.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this session by defining what constitutes a computing innovation. Teachers should write the core definition on the whiteboard: an innovation that includes a computer or program code as an integral part of its functionality. The central theme of this session is that while software and hardware are technical, their ultimate value lies in how they transform human interaction, collaboration, and basic infrastructure. This is critical because AP CSP students must understand that computing does not exist in a vacuum; every line of code has a downstream human effect.

To build intuition, we use a whiteboard diagram showcasing a centralized cloud database connected to three distinct nodes: healthcare, education, and disaster response. The teacher will trace how real-time data sharing completely transforms these sectors. For instance, in healthcare, instead of waiting days for mailed paper records, cloud-based electronic health records (EHRs) allow a specialist across the globe to view an MRI scan instantly, potentially saving a patient's life during an emergency. We emphasize that the underlying logic here is the reduction of latency—moving from asynchronous, high-latency physical communication to synchronous, low-latency digital sharing.

Next, the teacher will address a common misconception: students often mistake any modern physical invention (like a standard mechanical bicycle) for a computing innovation. We must explicitly point out that for an innovation to be classified as a 'computing innovation' under the AP framework, it must rely on active data processing, algorithms, or digital hardware. For example, a smart sharing bicycle with GPS tracking and an app backend is a computing innovation, whereas a traditional gear bicycle is not. Highlighting this distinction early prevents students from selecting invalid examples during their own assessments and exams.

We then move to an interactive reflection task. The teacher will ask students to identify how real-time collaboration platforms (like shared documents or distributed design tools) have shifted the workplace from localized, isolated efforts to global, collaborative environments. By asking students to outline the positive impacts of these cloud-based systems on global collaboration, we reveal whether they can connect high-level technological features (like cloud syncing and concurrency control) to tangible human benefits (such as cross-time-zone team operations and rapid remote consensus).

tasks: List three sectors transformed by real-time cloud data sharing, and explain the positive impacts on each.

sessions.title: Harmful and Unintended Effects
sessions.description: Examine how innovations can lead to unintended consequences, such as job losses or social polarization.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Begin the session by challenging the common assumption that technology is inherently neutral or that negative outcomes are solely the work of malicious actors. On the center of the whiteboard, write the phrase 'The Law of Unintended Consequences in Software.' Explain that when a computing innovation scales to millions of users, the sheer volume of interactions creates emergent behaviors that developers could not easily simulate in a closed testing environment. The core focus of this session is to train students to look past the marketing promise of an innovation and critically trace its systemic side effects.

Draw a horizontal split on the whiteboard. On the top half, map out the algorithmic feedback loop of modern social media recommendation engines. Start with the developer's benign objective: 'Keep users engaged by showing them content they like.' Walk through the logical chain: to maximize engagement, the system tracks watch time and clicks, then serves increasingly similar content. Introduce the concept of the 'echo chamber' and 'filter bubbles.' Explain how this feedback loop unintentionally isolates users from diverse viewpoints, driving social polarization. Point out a key misconception here: students often think polarization is a deliberate feature programmed by developers, whereas it is actually an unintended emergent property of optimizing for simple engagement metrics.

Transition to the economic dimension of unintended consequences, focusing on workforce displacement. Explain that while automation and algorithmic scheduling increase operational efficiency and lower consumer costs, they also create immediate friction for workers whose skills are suddenly automated. Draw a balance scale on the board to illustrate this trade-off: on one side, lower costs and faster services for the public; on the other, sudden job instability and the demanding requirement for rapid workforce retraining. Emphasize that the ethical responsibility of a developer includes anticipating these systemic shifts rather than dismissing them as external economic factors.

Conclude with an interactive whiteboard walkthrough analyzing the ride-share paradox to prepare students for the practice task. Sketch a simple city grid. Show how an app designed to optimize ride-matching aims to reduce personal car ownership and traffic. Then, trace the real-world behavioral shift: because ride-sharing becomes incredibly cheap and convenient, users stop taking subways or walking, transferring their transit habits to individual cars. Additionally, show how drivers 'deadheading'—cruising slowly while empty, waiting for their next ride request—adds extra physical vehicles to the road. This visual demonstration clearly illustrates how a tool designed to reduce congestion can counterintuitively paralyze city infrastructure, proving that local optimization does not always equal global efficiency.

tasks: Explain how an app intended to match local ride-shares could unintentionally worsen local traffic congestion.

sessions.title: Evaluating Effects on Different Groups
sessions.description: Analyze how computing advancements affect diverse demographic, geographic, and socioeconomic groups differently.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this session by addressing a major conceptual shift for our students: moving beyond a binary 'good vs. bad' view of technology to examine how identical computing innovations distribute their benefits and burdens unevenly across society. This transition is crucial for AP CSP students to build the analytical tools needed for socio-technical evaluations. We introduce the core framework of evaluating impact across three distinct axes: demographic, geographic, and socioeconomic lines. Using the whiteboard, we split the board into these three categories, prompting students to understand that an innovation designed with 'average' users in mind often fails to account for structural differences like high-speed internet availability or historical biases embedded in training data.

To anchor this theory, we transition into an interactive whiteboard walkthrough centered around an automated AI-driven hiring system. First, we outline the logistical chain of the system: a candidate uploads a resume, a video interview is analyzed for 'emotional sentiment' and 'confidence metrics' using natural language processing, and an automated algorithm ranks the applicants. On the whiteboard, we draw a clear dividing line between a candidate from a well-connected urban tech hub and a candidate from a remote rural community. By visually mapping out their paths, we reveal the hidden geographic and socioeconomic assumptions built into the software. For instance, the rural candidate may face issues with broadband latency that glitch the video interview, or their resume may lack specific buzzwords from local vocational schools that the algorithm hasn't been trained to recognize.

A key pedagogical trap to prevent during this lecture is the 'neutral technology' misconception—the idea that because a computer program uses math to grade candidates, it is naturally objective. We must explicitly point out to students that algorithms are trained on historical human decisions. If a hiring system is trained on historical data from a company that previously hired mostly urban, high-income males, the software will mathematically institutionalize those exact historical biases under the guise of an objective algorithm. We show how this negatively impacts demographic groups who are underrepresented in the training data, demonstrating that software logic is never truly isolated from human bias.

We transition to the hands-on practice phase, where students will draft a short impact assessment for this exact automated hiring scenario. Instead of just listing pros and cons, students are guided to identify the specific failure modes of the automated pipeline for both rural and urban cohorts, and then write down concrete technical and operational adjustments. We explain to the teachers that this exercise is designed to reveal whether students can identify the hidden dependencies of computing innovations—such as reliable high-bandwidth infrastructure and representative training data—and translate these technical dependencies into social impacts. We close the session by reviewing how developers can implement fairer validation testing before deployment.

tasks: Write a short impact assessment for an automated hiring system, outlining its effects on rural versus urban candidates.

sessions.title: Balancing Benefits and Risks
sessions.description: Examine how developers, regulators, and users weigh trade-offs when launching new technologies.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this final session of Unit 5 by establishing the central tension of modern technology design: the constant friction between maximizing functional utility, such as personalized user experiences, and preserving fundamental human rights, such as data privacy. As a concept-first public lecture, we want to frame this not as a technical bug to be solved with more code, but as a deliberate, structural trade-off. To ground this concept, draw a simple balancing scale on the whiteboard. Label one side 'Personalization/Convenience' and the other side 'Privacy/Security'. Explain that every modern computing innovation sits somewhere on this fulcrum, and a shift toward one inevitably compromises the other.

Walk students through the mechanics of a personalized recommendation engine to explain why this trade-off exists. To suggest the perfect song, article, or product, an algorithm must continuously ingest, analyze, and retain massive amounts of user behavior data, ranging from location history to precise interaction timestamps. The core teaching point here is that high personalization requires high data transparency. However, storing this rich, granular data creates a massive honeypot for malicious actors and exposes users to tracking, profiling, and unintended data leaks. Teachers should actively warn against the common misconception that we can achieve 'perfectly personalized' systems with 'zero data collection'; explain that some level of data sacrifice is mathematically and logically required for predictive features to function.

Introduce a concrete classroom scenario to anchor the practice task: imagine a local health-tracking application that wants to provide highly customized fitness plans. To do this, it requests continuous GPS tracking and daily biometric logs. Now, pivot the whiteboard to present an alternative design decision: the development team decides to store and process all biometric data strictly locally on the user's device, using randomized aggregation to blur GPS locations before they ever reach the central cloud servers. This design choice explicitly sacrifices raw personalization accuracy because the server cannot build a perfect, real-time profile of the individual. However, it drastically minimizes the risk of a centralized data breach.

Guide the classroom in defending this privacy-first design choice. The pedagogical goal of this exercise is to help students articulate that sacrificing marginal algorithmic accuracy is a proactive defense mechanism. By minimizing data collection at the source, developers eliminate the threat vector of a centralized database compromise. If the cloud servers are breached, there is simply no sensitive user history there to be stolen. This shift from reactive security—like hoping encryption holds—to proactive architectural minimization is the hallmark of ethical technology development.

Conclude by discussing how this trade-off is negotiated in the real world through regulatory frameworks like GDPR or CCPA, and how developers must learn to treat privacy as a non-negotiable constraint rather than an afterthought. This positions the students to view themselves not just as programmers who write functional code, but as architects who make intentional ethical choices about what data their applications have the right to possess.

tasks: Defend a design decision that sacrifices raw user personalization in order to enhance user privacy protection.

lectures.title: Access, Bias, and Ethical Responsibility
lectures.description: Examine how systematic biases, the digital divide, and crowdsourced solutions impact equity and accessibility in modern computing.

sessions.title: The Digital Divide
sessions.description: Examine global inequalities in high-speed internet and hardware access, and discuss initiatives working to bridge these gaps.
sessions.sessionOutline:
To introduce the session on the Digital Divide, begin by asking a simple question to prime the students' intuition: if you have a computer but no access to reliable, high-speed internet, is the machine truly a window to the modern digital world? Map this on the physical whiteboard by sketching two environments: an urban neighborhood with short fiber-optic links and cellular towers every few hundred meters, and a rural or remote school dependent on copper telephone lines or unstable satellite links. Emphasize that the digital divide is not just a binary of 'having a computer' or 'not having one,' but a spectrum of quality, speed, bandwidth, and affordability. This reframing is crucial for students to realize that access is systemic and geographic, not merely personal.

Now, build the core logic chain. Draw a direct line from infrastructure limits to educational and economic impacts. Explain that the cost of laying fiber-optic cables over long distances to sparsely populated areas prevents internet service providers (ISPs) from investing in rural broadband. Show how this lack of physical infrastructure leads to an educational gap: rural schools struggle to offer digital curriculum updates, cloud-based research tools, or online AP prep, while urban schools with rich fiber access take them for granted. The key takeaway is that infrastructure determines access, and unequal access compound historical social inequities. Address a common student misconception here: many think mobile phones and cellular data have completely solved this. Clarify on the whiteboard that mobile data is often capped, expensive per gigabyte, and inadequate for heavy computing tasks like programming, large file transfers, or attending virtual classes.

Transition into a brief whiteboard mapping of current public and private initiatives working to bridge these gaps. Sketch out the differences between physical fiber expansion, government-subsidized broadband plans for low-income households, and high-capacity low-Earth-orbit satellite constellations. Note how each solution has trade-offs—for instance, satellites offer coverage but introduce latency and weather interference, while laying fiber is expensive and slow.

Conclude by running a reflective practice moment. Ask students to identify and contrast two specific infrastructure factors—such as physical terrain/population density affecting fiber deployment and the financial feasibility of ISP hardware maintenance—that prevent a rural school from matching the connectivity of an urban counterpart. Guide the students to see that solving the digital divide requires analyzing physical, geographic, and economic barriers, establishing a strong foundation for understanding how computing innovations affect society unevenly.

tasks: Identify two infrastructure factors that contribute to the digital divide between rural and urban schools.

sessions.title: Bias in Computing
sessions.description: Investigate how training algorithms on historical human data can perpetuate or amplify societal biases.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this session by addressing a widespread misconception among students: the belief that algorithms are inherently objective and neutral because they rely on mathematics and logic. To disrupt this assumption, the instructor should write a simple formula on the board: 'Algorithm + Data = Decision.' Explain that while the logical formula (the algorithm) may be mathematically consistent, the data used to train it is produced by humans, carries historical prejudices, and reflects existing societal inequalities. By introducing this concept-first framework, we establish that computers do not possess moral judgment; they merely find patterns in the history we feed them.

To ground this concept, we walk through a concrete case study of a machine learning model designed for credit card approvals or loan decisions. The instructor should sketch a simplified pipeline on the whiteboard showing historical training data (containing past lending decisions from an era with systemic redlining or gender discrimination) feeding into a training engine to generate a predictive model. If the historic training data reflects a past where a certain demographic was systematically denied loans, the algorithm will mathematically identify membership in that demographic as a high-risk factor. It is vital to emphasize that the algorithm is not 'broken' in a technical sense; it is actually performing its pattern-matching task perfectly, which is precisely why it perpetuates and amplifies historic bias into the future.

Next, we tackle the subtle ways bias sneaks into algorithms even when developers explicitly remove protected attributes like race, gender, or age. The instructor should introduce the concept of 'proxy variables.' On the whiteboard, draw connections between a protected attribute (e.g., race) and seemingly neutral features (e.g., zip codes, high school attended, or retail shopping habits). Explain how a machine learning model can easily reconstruct the missing protected attribute using these highly correlated proxies. This reveals a common pitfall in naive algorithm design: simply deleting a sensitive column does not make a system unbiased. Teachers should warn students that algorithms are highly efficient at discovering these backdoor pathways, which can lead to unintentional but systematic discrimination.

To consolidate this understanding, transition to the practice task where students analyze a simulated credit approval algorithm. The instructor should present a scenario where a bank uses automated software to screen loan applicants, utilizing training data from the past forty years. Ask the students to identify specific historical biases that might be hidden in that data and explain how those biases manifest in modern automated rejections. This exercise is designed to reveal whether students can link historical human discrimination to algorithmic outcomes, moving past the surface-level definition of bias to diagnose structural flaws in data-driven decision-making.

tasks: Analyze a credit approval algorithm to identify how historical bias in the training data could impact modern loan decisions.

sessions.title: Crowdsourcing
sessions.description: Explore how developers use internet-connected crowds to gather funding, code reviews, and distributed solutions.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this session by introducing crowdsourcing as a modern, decentralized model that leverages the collective power of the internet to solve complex problems, secure funding, or compile vast amounts of data. To build an intuitive foundation for students, we draw a clear distinction between traditional centralized problem-solving—where a single closed group of experts does all the work—and crowdsourcing, which opens the doors to distributed, public participation. The core idea to emphasize is that the internet acts as a giant coordinator, transforming what would be an impossible administrative bottleneck into an organized, parallel effort. We will contrast examples like a traditional encyclopedia written by selected scholars with Wikipedia, built and maintained by millions of global contributors, to show how scale changes the speed and scope of knowledge creation.

Next, we shift the whiteboard to look at how developers use this paradigm practically, focusing on three primary pillars of crowdsourcing: funding (crowdfunding), quality assurance (distributed code reviews and bug bounties), and distributed problem-solving. For funding, we sketch how small, individual micro-donations bypass traditional venture capital barriers to launch niche software projects. For code reviews and open-source contributions, we explain the concept that 'with enough eyeballs, all bugs are shallow.' It is vital here to address a major student misconception: that crowdsourced projects are chaotic, low-quality, or completely unmoderated. The instructor should illustrate how successful crowdsourcing requires strict algorithmic filtering, user reputation systems, and validation pipelines. Without automated checks or moderator dashboards, crowdsourcing quickly devolves into noise and vandalism.

To bring this concept into a practical scenario, we introduce the transit app tracking problem. If a city tries to track every bus manually, they must install expensive GPS tracking hardware in every single vehicle, maintain the servers, and handle any connection dropouts. This is a centralized bottleneck. Instead, a modern public transit app can use crowdsourcing by accessing the real-time GPS locations and movement speeds of thousands of daily commuters riding those buses. The teacher will sketch a simple flow on the whiteboard: Commuter devices -> Anonymized location data streams -> App servers -> Aggragated real-time bus arrival estimations. We discuss how the system filters out outlier data—such as a user who gets off the bus and starts walking—to ensure accuracy.

Finally, we engage the class in a practice exercise based on this transit app scenario. The task is for students to outline how such an app can safely and reliably collect this data. This exercise is designed to reveal whether students understand the trade-offs of crowdsourcing, specifically highlighting issues of data privacy (how to track bus movement without exposing individual user identities) and data validation (how to ignore bad data points). We wrap up the session by highlighting how this collective intelligence enables apps to be incredibly dynamic, setting up the logical transition to our next session on citizen science, where this crowd-driven model is scaled to serve global scientific discovery.

tasks: Outline how a public transit app can use crowdsourcing to update bus arrival times in real time.

sessions.title: Citizen Science
sessions.description: Examine how public participation and shared data collection help scientific research scale beyond traditional laboratories.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this session by defining 'Citizen Science' on the whiteboard as a powerful subset of crowdsourcing, specifically where public volunteers contribute to scientific research projects. To build instant intuition, contrast a traditional lab setup—where a small team of scientists is constrained by geography, funding, and time—with the decentralized power of global citizen networks. The core shift to emphasize is how modern computing infrastructure (cheap smartphones, GPS, and cellular networks) turns ordinary individuals into a vast, distributed network of scientific sensors. This concept is vital for the AP CSP framework because it illustrates how the internet and mobile technologies democratize data collection at a scale previously deemed impossible.

To map out the logical pipeline of how this works, sketch a step-by-step workflow on the whiteboard using a real-world scenario: tracking bird migration patterns. Draw a diagram starting with a single hiker taking a photo of a rare bird. Explain the data payload of this action: the image itself, plus crucial metadata (exact GPS coordinates and timestamp). Show how this local data point is uploaded to a centralized scientific database, where it joins thousands of other entries. Explain that the scientific value does not come from a single photo, but from the aggregated visualization of these data points across a map, revealing migration corridors, timing shifts due to climate change, and population densities in real-time.

Address a major student misconception here: the belief that data collected by untrained citizens must be too noisy, inaccurate, or low-quality to be scientifically useful. We tackle this head-on by explaining how modern software platforms incorporate validation layers. Sketch out validation techniques on the whiteboard, such as peer review (where other users must confirm the species identification), algorithmic filtering (using machine learning computer vision to verify the image matches the bird claimed), and statistical outlier removal. This teaches students that data quality is managed through software engineering design, not just expert-only data collection.

We transition into the practice phase by asking students to trace the journey of these bird photos from capturing to mapping. This exercise checks if they understand how individual contributions scale into a macro-level dataset. By analyzing this specific application, students learn to articulate the relationship between crowd participation, metadata integrity, and the ultimate scientific insight generated. Conclude by reinforcing that citizen science represents a monumental shift from localized, private research to an open, collaborative model of human-centric computing.

tasks: Explain how citizen science projects use thousands of mobile phone camera photos to map global bird migrations.

sessions.title: Ethical Responsibilities of Developers
sessions.description: Analyze standard codes of conduct and the responsibilities software engineers have when deploying public algorithms.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this session by establishing the core premise of software engineering ethics: code is not neutral, and the decisions programmers make have immediate, real-world consequences on people's safety, privacy, and livelihood. Rather than viewing software development as a purely technical exercise of optimizing algorithms or meeting client deadlines, we introduce the concept of professional responsibility as outlined by major industry organizations like the ACM (Association for Computing Machinery) and the IEEE. On the whiteboard, draw a simple conceptual triangle labeled 'The Developer's Triad of Duty' with three vertices: the Client, the User, and the Public. Many novice developers make the mistake of believing their sole duty is to the client who pays them. We must explicitly unpack this misconception, explaining that professional codes of conduct universally place the public's well-being, safety, and privacy as the absolute highest priority, even when it directly conflicts with a client's immediate business desires.

To ground these abstract guidelines in concrete practice, we transition to a whiteboard scenario involving a shipping and logistics application that has just been prepared for deployment. Walk through a timeline where the testing team discovers a critical security vulnerability—specifically, an unencrypted database connection that exposes customers' home addresses and delivery schedules to anyone on the same local network. Draw a flowchart showing the standard release pipeline versus the ethical intervention path. Explain how the pressure to meet a 'go-live' date can create a conflict of interest. We guide the class through analyzing this scenario under the ACM Code of Ethics, prompting them to identify which specific principles apply, such as avoiding harm, being honest and trustworthy, and respecting privacy. This teaches students how to systematically evaluate professional dilemmas rather than relying on vague intuition.

Next, we address a common misconception among developers: the belief that they can simply 'patch it later' without disclosing the risk, or that they are shielded from responsibility because their manager ordered them to ship the code anyway. We use the whiteboard to model the chain of accountability. If a system is deployed with known, unmitigated vulnerabilities, the developers who knowingly signed off on it share moral and professional liability. Explain how to document and escalate these issues constructively within an organization. We draw a step-by-step escalation path on the board: from documenting the bug in a tracker, to proposing a mitigation plan, to formally notifying stakeholders, and finally understanding when whistleblowing or refusing to sign off on a release becomes an ethical necessity.

We then transition to an interactive practice exercise. Present the students with a simulated internal memo from a shipping app company's executive team, urging the developers to bypass the final security audit of a new location-tracking feature to beat a competitor's release date. Ask the students to write a brief, professional response applying the ethical guidelines we just discussed. This task is designed to reveal whether students can translate theoretical ethical codes into professional, assertive communication. It exposes whether they succumb to authority bias or if they can successfully prioritize public safety and data protection over corporate pressure. We conclude by reviewing their responses, highlighting how framing security as a long-term business asset and a non-negotiable public duty is the mark of a truly professional software engineer.

tasks: Apply professional ethics guidelines to a scenario where a software team discovers security holes in a shipping app.

lectures.description: Learn to safeguard digital assets. Explore tracking, multi-factor authentication, public-key encryption, malware, and intellectual property laws.

sessions.title: Personal Data and Digital Tracking
sessions.description: Trace how actions online leave digital footprints through cookies, geolocations, and tracking pixels.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin the lecture by introducing the foundational concept of a digital footprint. Students often struggle to conceptualize how intangible actions online translate into permanent, structured physical records on remote servers. To build this intuition, the teacher should sketch a simple timeline on the whiteboard showing a user's progress through a single web browsing session. Contrast 'active' data sharing—such as filling out a form or posting a comment—with 'passive' data collection, where background systems collect metadata without direct user interaction. Emphasize that in modern web ecosystems, passive collection is far more ubiquitous and highly valuable for profiling behavior.

Next, the teacher transitions to the mechanics of tracking, starting with HTTP cookies. Explain that because HTTP is fundamentally a stateless protocol—meaning it treats every request as completely independent with no memory of past interactions—websites need a mechanism to remember who you are. Draw a client-server exchange showing how a server sends a 'Set-Cookie' header and how the browser automatically includes this small text file in every subsequent request. This is the moment to address a critical AP CSP distinction: the difference between first-party cookies, which keep you logged in or preserve your shopping cart, and third-party cookies, which are set by ad networks embedded in the page to track your movement across unrelated websites.

We then expand the tracking toolkit on the whiteboard by introducing tracking pixels and geolocation. Sketch a webpage containing an invisible 1x1 pixel image hosted on an ad server. Explain that when the browser requests this tiny image, it inadvertently transmits headers containing the user's IP address, device type, user-agent string, and referrer URL to that third party. Use this to explain geolocation: how an IP address can pinpoint a user's general geographic region, whereas GPS-enabled mobile devices can broadcast precise coordinates, creating a detailed physical-digital trace. This sequence helps students understand that tracking is not dependent on a single file but is an interconnected web of hardware signals and software requests.

To apply this knowledge, the teacher leads a detailed walkthrough of a single product search on an online shopping platform. On the whiteboard, draw a diagram of a user searching for 'running shoes.' Map out each point of collection: the initial search query, the click-through rates of specific models, the duration spent hovering over particular colors, the addition to the cart, and the eventual abandonment or purchase. Point out that even without logging into an account, the site associates these actions with a unique device fingerprint or temporary cookie ID. This exercise is designed to demystify data harvesting and show how raw, minute user actions are compiled into structured consumer profiles.

During this discussion, the teacher must proactively dismantle common student misconceptions, most notably the myth of 'Incognito' or 'Private' browsing modes. Explain clearly that private browsing simply prevents the local device from saving browsing history, search history, and cookies after the session is closed. It does not mask the user's identity from the internet service provider, the school network administrator, or the destination servers themselves. Visualizing this on the board by drawing a local computer boundary separate from the external network boundary helps students understand where privacy boundaries actually begin and end.

Finally, conclude the session by introducing the practice task, where students will map out the points of personal data collection during their own hypothetical online search. The goal of this exercise is to shift students from passive technology consumers to analytical systems-thinkers. By identifying the exact technical mechanisms—such as tracking pixels loaded during search autocomplete, or geolocations used to suggest local store inventory—students build a robust mental model of digital tracking that serves as the perfect springboard for discussing data security and policy in the next sessions.

tasks: Map out the points of personal data collection that occur during a single product search on an online shopping site.

sessions.title: Data Privacy
sessions.description: Contrast security safeguards with tracking features, analyzing when users must choose between privacy and convenience.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this session by addressing the core tension of modern digital life: the constant trade-off between privacy and convenience. To make this abstract concept concrete for students, we draw a clear physical analogy on the board. Imagine a physical journal kept under a mattress versus a shared digital document hosted on a server. The physical journal is completely private but lacks search capabilities, backups, and collaborative access. The digital document offers immediate synchronization across devices and easy sharing, but requires trusting a third-party server administrator with the content. This juxtaposition sets up our operational definition of data privacy as the user's ability to control how, when, and to what extent their personal information is collected, processed, and shared with others, distinct from security, which is the technical safeguarding of that data from unauthorized access.

Next, we transition to our primary whiteboard visualization comparing local data storage with cloud data synchronization. We sketch out two distinct technical architectures. On the left side of the board, we represent 'Local Storage' as an isolated device icon (such as a laptop or phone) where files reside solely on physical solid-state drives. We trace the logical flow of data: it never leaves the local network, meaning zero exposure to external corporate entities, no tracking of usage habits across platforms, and complete control over physical access. However, we immediately illustrate the severe operational trade-offs: if the device experiences mechanical failure, is lost, or is stolen, the data is gone forever. This visual framing helps students realize that absolute privacy often shifts the burden of data protection and disaster recovery entirely onto the individual.

On the right side of the board, we sketch the 'Cloud Synchronization' architecture. We draw a dotted line representing the internet, connecting the individual device to a remote server cluster. We map out the immense convenience benefits: automated real-time backups, effortless access from any device worldwide, and powerful server-side indexing. However, we explicitly highlight the privacy trade-offs using red arrows pointing from the server to third-party databases. Even with robust encryption, cloud providers often collect metadata, such as login locations, active hours, file sizes, and structural directories. We must warn students of a common misconception here: many believe that using 'Private Browsing' or 'Incognito' modes stops cloud services from synchronizing and profiling their account data once they are logged in. We emphasize that application-level synchronization bypasses browser privacy settings entirely.

To cement these concepts, we introduce a reflective practice task. We ask students to analyze a scenario where a user must decide between hosting their personal photo library on an external hard drive in their desk drawer versus syncing it automatically to a major cloud provider. We direct students to evaluate this scenario through two specific lenses: the risk of physical loss and the risk of unauthorized profile building by corporate data brokers. This exercise is designed to reveal whether students can move past the oversimplified 'cloud is good, local is bad' binary and instead articulate how a choice that maximizes convenience (automated cloud sync) systematically degrades privacy, while a choice maximizing privacy (local storage) dramatically increases the operational risk of permanent data loss.

tasks: Compare privacy trade-offs between local data storage and cloud data synchronization.

sessions.title: Authentication
sessions.description: Understand multi-factor authentication, password hashing, and biometric security steps.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this whiteboard session by drawing a stark contrast between identification (stating who you are) and authentication (proving who you are). Many students mistakenly conflate these two steps, assuming that entering a username is part of the security proof, when in fact it is just a label. The teacher should sketch a simple gatekeeper scenario on the board: the user presents an ID card (identity assertion) and must then provide a secret or token to open the gate (authentication). This establishes the foundational logic that authentication is the bedrock of system trust. It prevents unauthorized impersonation by demanding verified proof of identity.

Next, the teacher introduces the three classic 'factors' of authentication, visually organizing them into a three-column table on the whiteboard: 'Something you know' (passwords, PINs), 'Something you have' (physical keys, hardware tokens, smartphones receiving SMS), and 'Something you are' (biometrics like fingerprints or facial recognition). It is crucial to address a common learner misconception here: simply requiring two passwords or a password and a security question does not constitute Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA) because both belong to the same 'Something you know' category. To truly achieve MFA, a system must demand credentials from at least two distinct categories. The teacher should trace a real-world login flow on the board showing how combining a knowledge factor (password) with a possession factor (a temporary push notification to a smartphone) creates an exponential leap in security.

To deepen technical intuition, the teacher will pivot to how servers handle the 'Something you know' factor without compromising security. On the board, trace the flow of a password from creation to storage. Explain that servers do not store passwords in plaintext; doing so would be a catastrophic single point of failure if the database were hacked. Instead, introduce the concept of a cryptographic hash function—a mathematical one-way street. Draw an input (the password) going into a 'hash function block' and emerging as an unrecognizable, fixed-length string of hexadecimal characters (the hash). Explain that when a user logs in, the server hashes the incoming password and compares it to the stored hash. If they match, entry is granted. The teacher should explicitly warn against the misconception that hashes can be easily 'decrypted' back into passwords, reinforcing that hashing is a one-way mathematical function designed to protect credentials even during database leaks.

To wrap up, the teacher guides students through an interactive practice scenario to test their understanding. On the whiteboard, illustrate a scenario where an attacker successfully steals a user's password through a phishing email. Ask the students: why does MFA prevent this attacker from gaining access, and where exactly does the security chain hold? The discussion should reveal that because the attacker only possesses the knowledge factor (the stolen password) but lacks the physical possession factor (the user's physical phone or hardware token to approve the MFA prompt), the authentication sequence fails at the second gate. This concrete scenario reinforces the practical utility of MFA, demonstrating to students that layered security is designed specifically to withstand the compromise of any single factor.

tasks: Explain why multi-factor authentication keeps accounts secure even when a password is stolen.

sessions.title: Encryption
sessions.description: Learn the math behind cryptography. Compare symmetric encryption with public-key (asymmetric) encryption.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this whiteboard-driven session by establishing the fundamental necessity of cryptography in a digital world where information constantly traverses public networks. The lecture starts with symmetric encryption, presenting it as the historical foundation of secure communication where a single shared secret key is used for both encryption and decryption. To ground this concept, we draw a clear, physical-world analogy on the whiteboard: a lockbox that requires the exact same physical key to lock and unlock. The primary teaching goal here is to help students appreciate that while symmetric encryption is computationally fast and highly secure once the key is shared, it suffers from a fatal flaw—the Key Exchange Problem. We pose a critical question to the class: 'If you and a friend want to communicate securely over the internet, how do you securely share the key in the first place without someone intercepting it?' This question serves as the intellectual bridge to asymmetric methods.

To build early concrete intuition, we transition to our first interactive practice. On the whiteboard, we write out the standard English alphabet paired with their index values (A=0, B=1, ... Z=25). We lead the students through a live simulation of a Caesar Cipher, which is a classic substitution symmetric cipher. We select a shifting key, such as three, and demonstrate how the plaintext message 'CAT' transforms into the ciphertext 'FDW' by shifting each letter forward by three places. We then show how decryption works by performing the exact reverse operation using the same key of three. During this exercise, we explicitly address a common student misconception: many beginners believe that symmetric encryption is insecure simply because a shift cipher is easy to crack. We clarify that the vulnerability of the Caesar cipher lies in its small key space, whereas modern symmetric algorithms like AES use highly complex keys that are mathematically unbreakable within a reasonable timeframe. The real vulnerability of symmetric encryption is not the strength of the algorithm, but the logistical nightmare of distributing the shared secret key securely.

This limitation unlocks the need for Public-Key (Asymmetric) Encryption. We introduce this revolutionary concept on the whiteboard using a powerful visual analogy of a mailbox. Anyone can walk up to a mailbox and slide a letter through the slot—this represents the Public Key, which is openly distributed and used by anyone to encrypt messages. However, only the postal carrier who holds the physical key can open the back of the mailbox to retrieve and read the letters—this represents the Private Key, which is kept strictly secret by the receiver and is the only key capable of decrypting the message. We draw these two keys on the whiteboard as a mathematically linked pair, emphasizing that a message encrypted with the Public Key can only be decrypted by its corresponding Private Key, and not even the sender can decrypt it once it is locked.

Next, we dive into the math behind this magic. Since this is a derivation-focused session, we break down how one-way functions make asymmetric encryption possible. We illustrate the concept of modular arithmetic—often called 'clock arithmetic'—on the board. We show how some operations are incredibly easy to compute in one direction (such as multiplying two massive prime numbers), but computationally infeasible to reverse (factoring the resulting product back into its original primes) without a special piece of auxiliary information known as the 'trapdoor.' We walk through a simplified, small-scale mathematical model to demystify how these keys are structurally paired, ensuring students understand that the security of public-key cryptography relies on the extreme computational difficulty of reversing these mathematical functions.

We wrap up the session by comparing the practical applications of both encryption models. We explain that because public-key encryption is mathematically complex and computationally expensive, modern internet security actually uses a hybrid approach. For instance, when establishing an HTTPS connection to a website, asymmetric cryptography is used solely to securely agree upon a symmetric key, and once that secure connection is established, the faster symmetric encryption takes over for the remainder of the session. We warn students to avoid the common trap of thinking that asymmetric encryption completely replaces symmetric encryption; instead, they must understand that they work together to balance speed and security on the modern internet.

tasks: Simulate encrypting and decrypting a message using a basic Caesar Cipher key structure.

sessions.title: Malware and Social Engineering
sessions.description: Identify digital vulnerabilities, including phishing, keyloggers, ransomware, and social engineering tricks.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this whiteboard session by reframing security away from raw mathematics and toward the human factor. Draw a simple diagram on the board: a massive, impenetrable iron gate representing public-key encryption and firewalls, but right next to it, a small turnstile representing human actions. This visual anchors the concept of social engineering—the psychological manipulation of people into performing actions or divulging confidential information. Explain to the class that even the most secure network protocols can be completely bypassed if an authorized user is tricked into handing over their credentials or executing malicious software. This sets up a crucial paradigm shift for students: computer security is as much about human behavior and verification processes as it is about software patches.

Next, transition to cataloging the technical tools that bad actors deploy once they exploit this human vulnerability. Use the whiteboard to contrast key malware concepts in a comparative grid. Define a keylogger as software that silently records keystrokes to steal passwords, ransomware as malware that encrypts a victim's files and demands payment for the decryption key, and Trojan horses as malicious programs masquerading as benign software. Address a common student misconception here: many believe malware magically infects systems without any user interaction. Emphasize that most malware requires a trigger—like running an email attachment or clicking a deceptive link—to initiate its payload. This distinction is vital for understanding why user behavior is the primary target for attackers.

Now, focus deeply on phishing as the primary vehicle for delivering these payloads. On the whiteboard, draw a clear distinction between generic phishing and 'spear-phishing'. Explain that while generic phishing is a numbers game—sending millions of spam emails hoping a tiny fraction bite—spear-phishing is highly targeted and personalized. It leverages specific information about the victim, such as their job title, project names, or professional relationships, to craft an incredibly convincing lie. This distinction is highly relevant for AP Computer Science Principles because it highlights how personal data aggregated from digital footprints can be weaponized against individuals.

To apply this knowledge, draw a mock email interface directly on the whiteboard for a collaborative analysis exercise. The mock email should simulate a spear-phishing attempt targeting a school administrator: it should come from an address resembling the school board's domain (e.g., 'admin@school-board-portal.org' instead of '.gov' or '.edu'), address the target by their specific name, reference a real upcoming event, contain an urgent demand to update payroll details, and include a link masked as 'secure-portal-login'. Guide the class in dissecting this email step-by-step. Point out the psychological triggers used: authority, urgency, and fear of consequences. Show how to inspect the actual URL destination behind the hyperlinked text and look for subtle domain name spelling anomalies, teaching students how to run a systematic diagnostic of suspicious digital communications.

Conclude the session by discussing defensive countermeasures. Explain that while technical filters can catch obvious spam, defense-in-depth requires a combination of human skepticism and protocol-based verification. Introduce concepts like multi-factor authentication as the ultimate backstop against credential theft, explaining that even if a spear-phishing attack successfully steals a password, the attacker cannot gain access without the secondary physical token. This ties the current session directly back to previous discussions on security structures, leaving students with a holistic understanding of digital defense.

tasks: Analyze an email scenario to identify signs of a spear-phishing attack.

sessions.title: Intellectual Property and Software Licensing
sessions.description: Explore copyright, patents, Creative Commons licensing, and open-source models.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Begin the session by addressing the fundamental paradox of digital creations: they are trivial to copy perfectly at zero cost, yet they require immense time and effort to create. Introduce the concept of Intellectual Property (IP) as a framework designed to balance the public's access to innovation with the creator's right to control and profit from their work. Explain to students that as digital developers, they will find themselves on both sides of this coin—protecting their own creations while legally and ethically utilizing the work of others.

On the whiteboard, draw a clear distinction between Copyrights and Patents. Explain that copyright automatically protects the original, creative expression of an idea, such as the actual source code, design assets, and written documentation, the moment it is written down or saved. Contrast this with patents, which must be applied for and protect functional inventions, physical mechanisms, or novel utility methods. Correct the common developer misconception that copyrighting code prevents others from ever writing a program that performs the same function; clarify that copyright only stops others from copying your specific code, whereas a patent would protect the underlying process itself.

Transition from standard proprietary systems to open-source software (OSS) models. Demystify the widespread myth that open-source software is in the "public domain" or lacks copyright protection. Explain that open-source software is still copyrighted, but the creator uses that copyright to grant specific, generous permissions to the public—such as the right to view, modify, and redistribute the code. Highlight how open-source licensing fosters global collaboration, accelerates technological progress, and forms the infrastructure of modern web development.

Introduce the Creative Commons (CC) licensing framework as a flexible bridge between strict copyright and public domain. On the whiteboard, map out the four modular terms of Creative Commons: Attribution (BY), ShareAlike (SA), NonCommercial (NC), and NoDerivatives (ND). Spend extra time clarifying the logical tension between NoDerivatives and ShareAlike. Explain that NoDerivatives means a user can share the original work but cannot edit or remix it, while ShareAlike permits editing and remixing but forces the new creator to distribute their derivative work under the exact same licensing terms. Prevent confusion by stressing that these terms can be mixed and matched to suit the creator's exact goals.

Conclude with a practical diagnostic scenario to solidify this understanding. Present the students with a challenge: a developer wants to share a newly designed software library so that other engineers can freely adapt, build upon, and remix it, but the developer wants to ensure they receive credit and that any derived versions remain free and open under the same terms. Walk through the process of elimination on the board—rejecting NoDerivatives because remixing is encouraged, incorporating Attribution (BY) for credit, and selecting ShareAlike (SA) to enforce ongoing openness. This exercise tests the students' ability to translate design requirements into precise legal tools, preparing them for responsible digital citizenship.

tasks: Choose the correct Creative Commons license for a software asset to allow remixes while requiring attribution.
